n: Argentina — Abuelas de Plaza de Mayo: 140 stolen grandchildren identified
who: Argentine military regime (1976–83); military families and regime allies who received children
cover: Children were illegally adopted with their original identities hidden; many did not know they were adopted.
d: The Grandmothers of Plaza de Mayo were founded in 1977 to find children kidnapped with their disappeared parents or born to mothers in detention, who were passed for adoption to military families and regime allies. Their work led to the creation of Argentina's National Bank of Genetic Data. On 7 July 2025 they announced the 140th grandchild identified: a man born on 17 April 1977 at the clandestine centre 'La Escuelita' in Bahía Blanca after his parents were kidnapped in Cutral Có, Neuquén. The Grandmothers had found 97 grandchildren by 2008 and 133 by July 2023.

n: Ireland — Mother and Baby Homes Commission: 9,000 child deaths; adoptions abroad
place: 18 institutions incl. Tuam (Co. Galway), Bessborough (Cork), Sean Ross Abbey (Roscrea)
who: Religious orders (incl. Bon Secours Sisters), local authorities and the Irish state
cover: In May 2018 Tusla referred 126 cases of births falsely registered by the St Patrick's Guild adoption agency (illegal registrations that hid children's identities).
d: The Commission of Investigation's final report (published 12 January 2021) covered 14 mother and baby homes and 4 county homes. About 9,000 children died in them between 1922 and 1998, about one in seven births and about twice the general infant mortality rate. Several homes had been linked to illegal domestic and foreign adoptions, many to the United States. On 13 January 2021 Taoiseach Micheál Martin apologised for a 'profound generational wrong'. (The care agent may hold the home-conditions record; this record focuses on removals and adoptions.)

n: China — Hunan orphanages bought trafficked babies for adoption (2005 convictions)
place: Hengyang, Hunan (six orphanages); babies brought from Guangdong
who: Six state orphanages in Hunan; traffickers from Guangdong; local officials
d: Six Hunan orphanages were found buying infants from traffickers who brought them from Guangdong, placing nearly 1,000 children with domestic and foreign families between 2002 and 2005. In 2005, according to Xinhua, 23 civil officials were fired; three traffickers were sentenced to 15 years and six others to 3–13 years.

n: Uganda — European Adoption Consultants bribery scheme; judges sanctioned
who: European Adoption Consultants (Ohio, defunct); Ugandan lawyers and judges
cover: Bribes were paid to Ugandan judges and other officials to secure adoption orders.
d: Between 2013 and 2016 the Ohio agency European Adoption Consultants arranged the adoption of more than 30 Ugandan children by US families; families were promised their children would attend school in Kampala but they were taken to an unlicensed home. On 14 August 2020 a federal indictment charged two EAC employees and Ugandan lawyer Dorah Mirembe (allegations; presumed innocent); an earlier employee, Robin Longoria, pleaded guilty in August 2019 to bribing Ugandan officials. On 17–18 August 2020 the US State Department sanctioned Ugandan judges Moses Mukiibi and Wilson Musalu Musene and lawyers Mirembe and Patrick Ecobu.

n: India — Malaysian Social Services, Chennai: children kidnapped for adoption
who: Malaysian Social Services adoption agency
d: Police suspected the family running the Malaysian Social Services agency since 1991 of kidnapping and trafficking more than 350 children; in May 2005 Chennai police arrested three family members and six others. Children allegedly had their appearance changed and histories fabricated; officers found files for 120 children sent overseas. TIME reported in 2008 that Australian authorities had earlier warnings.

n: South Korea — Brothers Home children sent overseas for adoption
who: Brothers Home (Busan detention facility); receiving agencies named by AP incl. Holt International, Children's Home Society of Minnesota
d: Brothers Home was a state-backed facility where people deemed vagrants were confined and forced to work; the TRC recognised state culpability on 23 August 2022 and counted 657 deaths there 1975–1988. An AP investigation (November 2019) found Brothers Home organised the adoption of 19 children abroad in 1979–1986 and that six US agencies received children from it. In February 2025 the TRC confirmed at least 31 children were improperly sent overseas for adoption through the facility.

n: Haiti — New Life Children's Refuge: US missionaries try to take 33 children after earthquake
place: Calebasse and Le Citron, near Port-au-Prince → Dominican border
who: New Life Children's Refuge (Idaho Baptist missionaries) led by Laura Silsby
d: On 29 January 2010, after the earthquake, ten American Baptist missionaries were detained trying to take 33 Haitian children to the Dominican Republic without proper documentation; their interpreters said group members had spoken with the children's parents. They were charged on 4 February 2010 with kidnapping and criminal association. In February a judge released eight, concluding they had not knowingly committed a crime, and later a ninth; the kidnapping and criminal association charges were dropped. On 17 May 2010 the organiser, Laura Silsby, was convicted of arranging illegal travel under a 1980 law restricting movement out of Haiti and sentenced to the 3 months and 8 days she had already served.

n: Kenya — babies stolen and sold in Nairobi, incl. from a government hospital (BBC Africa Eye)
place: Nairobi (Mama Lucy Kibaki Hospital; Kayole street clinics)
who: Street child-snatchers working for a buyer; illegal street clinics; a clinical social worker at a government hospital
d: A year-long BBC Africa Eye investigation (November 2020) found children snatched from homeless mothers in Nairobi and sold for about £350–550, illegal street clinics selling newborns (one offered an unborn child for about £315 while paying the mother £70), and a clinical social worker at the government-run Mama Lucy Kibaki Hospital who sold an abandoned two-week-old boy to undercover reporters for 300,000 shillings (£2,000) using legitimate transfer paperwork. The reporters delivered all the children to a children's home. The BBC said the official appeared to keep his job and the clinic appeared to still operate.

n: Thailand — 'Baby 101' surrogate baby-breeding operation
who: Baby 101 company
d: In February 2011 Thai police freed 14 Vietnamese women, half of them pregnant, held in two Bangkok houses with passports confiscated by a company called Baby 101 that took orders from childless couples for newborns. A Taiwanese woman said to run the operation was charged with human trafficking; four said they had been tricked, and the health minister said some appeared to have been raped.

n: Norway — state investigation of illegal intercountry adoptions (2023–)
who: Norwegian state; private adoption organisations
d: Norway launched an investigation in 2023 into whether illegal or unethical practices occurred in intercountry adoptions and whether Norwegian officials failed to control them; the foreign ministry said it was 'aware of serious findings' (AP, 2024). Norway received 6,295 Korean children 1955–2008, and in 1974–75 Scandinavian diplomats pressed South Korea to keep sending children after it tried to stop. In September 2025 a Korean-born adoptee served notice of a lawsuit against the Norwegian state alleging her adoption was illegal (allegation).

n: Liberia — post-war orphanage boom and adoption fraud
who: Private orphanages and adoption facilitators
d: After the civil war ended in 2003 the number of private orphanages rose from 40 to 120. In 2005 the Hannah B. Williams Orphanage in Monrovia was closed and 89 of its 102 'orphans' returned to their families. A 2007 UNICEF/Holt International report found many children entered the adoption pipeline through fraud, including false promises to birth parents, and the UN Mission found unaccredited for-profit orphanages. Canada placed a moratorium on Liberian adoptions.

n: Malaysia — online baby-selling trade (Al Jazeera 101 East)
who: Online brokers; baby sellers
d: An undercover Al Jazeera 101 East investigation (24 November 2016) documented an online trade in which babies were advertised with photos and sold for thousands of dollars, with buyers choosing by gender, race and skin colour. Some babies went to couples wanting a child; others, it reported, were sold to traffickers. Immigrant sex workers who cannot legally bear children in Malaysia were among those giving up babies.

n: Northern Ireland Historical Institutional Abuse Inquiry (22 institutions, 1922–1995)
who: 22 children's homes and institutions run by the state, voluntary bodies and religious orders in Northern Ireland
d: The Hart Inquiry's 10-volume, roughly 2,300-page report, published 20 January 2017, examined abuse in 22 residential institutions in Northern Ireland between 1922 and 1995, reviewing hundreds of government and intelligence files. It found systemic failings and abuse including sexual abuse across state, voluntary and church-run homes and recommended redress and a public apology.

n: Medomsley Detention Centre, County Durham — Neville Husband and staff
who: Medomsley Detention Centre for young offenders (Home Office Prison Service)
cover: The Prisons and Probation Ombudsman (November 2025) found that knowledge of the abuse held by the Prison Service, police and Home Office was 'ignored and dismissed', families' complaints led to no action, and successive wardens were 'either complicit or incompetent'.
d: Medomsley held young male offenders from 1961 to 1988. Neville Husband, an officer who ran the kitchens, was convicted of sexual offences in 2003 and again in 2005 and died in 2010; the Ombudsman called him 'possibly the most prolific sex offender in British history'. Operation Seabrook (from 2013) identified 32 living suspects; five former officers were convicted in 2019 and another in 2023, eight former staff jailed in total. The Ombudsman's report of 12 November 2025, based on 8,000 documents and 74 witnesses, found the authorities failed in their duty to keep detainees safe.

n: Independent Inquiry into Child Sexual Abuse — final report (England and Wales)
place: England and Wales (inquiry based in London)
who: Institutions across England and Wales: local authority care, churches, schools, custodial institutions, political parties, police
d: IICSA published its final report in October 2022 after 19 investigation reports, 325 days of public hearings, more than 700 live witnesses and almost 1,000 written statements, and over 200,000 documents. More than 6,200 victims and survivors took part in its Truth Project. It made 107 recommendations, including mandatory reporting of child sexual abuse. Its investigations found institutional failures by councils, police, churches and government departments.

n: Lügde campsite abuse — youth office placed foster child with offender
who: Two men at a permanent campsite; youth welfare offices of Lippe and Hameln-Pyrmont; Lippe police
cover: Welfare authorities placed a foster girl with the main offender despite allegations about him. Police failed to act on repeated complaints, evidence disappeared from police archives, and a case worker manipulated and deleted files. The NRW parliamentary inquiry found 'authority failure' and said the men could have been stopped two years earlier.
d: On 5 September 2019 the Detmold regional court sentenced Andreas V. to 13 years and Mario S. to 12 years, both followed by preventive detention, for abusing 32 children at a campsite in Lügde from 1998 to 2018; police found 32,000 files of abuse material. Youth welfare authorities had placed a foster daughter with Andreas V. The North Rhine-Westphalia Landtag inquiry (interim report 24 March 2022) found failures by police and the youth offices of Lippe and Hameln-Pyrmont.

n: Swiss administrative detention and forced placements (incl. Verdingkinder)
kind: sexual abuse + forced labour + child removal
who: Swiss cantonal and municipal authorities; about 650 institutions
d: The Independent Expert Commission on Administrative Detention, set up under the Federal Act of 21 March 2014, presented its final report on 2 September 2019. It found more than 60,000 people were interned in about 650 institutions without court order, mainly from 1930 to 1981, and that victims were abused physically, psychologically and sexually. The Swiss government had apologised in 2010; a 2016 law created a CHF 25,000 'solidarity contribution' for victims of compulsory measures, including children placed as indentured farm labourers (Verdingkinder).

n: Norwegian children's homes and special schools 1945–1980 (NOU 2004:23)
who: Norwegian municipal children's homes and state special schools
d: The official report NOU 2004:23 'Barnehjem og spesialskoler under lupen' found neglect and abuse, in part of a serious nature and including sexual abuse, in children's homes and special schools between 1945 and 1980. Bergen and other municipalities ran their own investigations and compensation schemes; in 2005 the Storting committee recommended adapting the state 'rettferdsvederlag' scheme with payments up to NOK 300,000 and a lower burden of proof.

n: Indian Residential Schools — Truth and Reconciliation Commission and abuse claims
place: Canada (schools in every province and territory except NB, PEI and NL)
who: Government of Canada; schools operated by the Catholic, Anglican, United and Presbyterian churches
cover: Under the settlement, claimants' IAP records are to be destroyed after 19 September 2027 unless the claimant asks to keep or share them.
d: About 150,000 First Nations, Métis and Inuit children attended federally funded, church-run residential schools; the last closed in 1997. The Truth and Reconciliation Commission's final report (December 2015) documented 3,200 deaths and said the true number is much higher. By the end of 2014, 37,951 claims had been made for injuries from physical and sexual abuse and 30,939 resolved. The Independent Assessment Process received 38,276 claims in total; adjudicators awarded $2.14 billion to 23,431 claimants and the government compensated 4,415 more directly.

n: Grandview Training School for Girls, Galt, Ontario
who: Ontario provincial training school for girls (juvenile reformatory)
cover: Complaints of serious sexual abuse made by girls while at the school were reportedly ignored and never investigated.
d: Hundreds of women reported physical and sexual abuse while held as girls at the Grandview Training School, a government-run school for 'troubled' girls in Galt (now Cambridge), Ontario, which closed in 1976. Eight former staff members were charged and two were convicted. Earlier sources not re-checked for this map also cite an investigation by Ontario Provincial Police and Waterloo Regional Police after the abuse became public in 1991, a survivors' group of more than 300 women seeking compensation, and a 1999 apology by MPP Jim Flaherty in the Ontario legislature on the province's behalf (these three points not re-confirmed in this pass).

n: New Hampshire Youth Development Center, Manchester
who: State of New Hampshire Youth Development Center (juvenile detention)
d: More than 1,100 former residents of New Hampshire's state youth detention centre have sued over physical, sexual and emotional abuse spanning six decades, and 11 former state workers have been arrested. In the first trial, on 3 May 2024, a jury found the state negligent and awarded David Meehan, who went to police in 2017, $38 million. The state argued it was not liable for 'rogue' employees. A state settlement fund had paid $102 million on 206 claims by October 2024, with 448 more pending.

n: Youth residential treatment facilities — US Senate Finance Committee 2024
who: Universal Health Services, Acadia Healthcare, Devereux Advanced Behavioral Health, Vivant Behavioral Healthcare (incl. former Sequel facilities); funded by Medicaid and child welfare agencies
d: A two-year Senate Finance Committee investigation released on 12 June 2024 found that 'horrific instances of sexual abuse persist unremediated' inside residential treatment facilities for children run by four large companies, along with physical abuse, overuse of restraints and overmedication. Facilities often receive more than $1,200 per child per day from Medicaid; states including Oregon sent foster children to out-of-state facilities.

n: Parramatta Training School for Girls and Hay Institution — Royal Commission Case Study 7
place: Parramatta, New South Wales (and Hay, NSW)
who: NSW state child-welfare department; Parramatta Girls Home (Parramatta Training School for Girls), Hay Institution for Girls
cover: Most alleged perpetrators were never reported or investigated; some resigned or were dismissed after inquiries; no criminal charges were laid.
d: Parramatta Girls Home was a NSW state-run institution for girls from 1887 to 1974, many of them Aboriginal girls of the Stolen Generations. The Royal Commission's February 2014 hearing (Case Study 7, report October 2014) heard evidence about 11 men, most of them superintendents or deputies, accused of physical and sexual abuse. Most alleged perpetrators were never reported or investigated and no criminal charges were laid. A 2004 Senate inquiry had earlier taken statements from 20 former residents.

n: Royal Commission into the Protection and Detention of Children in the Northern Territory (Don Dale)
place: Don Dale Youth Detention Centre, Berrimah, Darwin, NT
who: Northern Territory Government youth detention and child protection systems
cover: A 2014 media release falsely said six boys had escaped when CCTV showed one; two earlier reports (January 2015 review and the August 2015 Children's Commissioner report) were not acted on.
d: The Royal Commission into the Protection and Detention of Children in the Northern Territory was set up in July 2016 after ABC Four Corners broadcast footage of boys at Don Dale being tear-gassed, hooded with spit hoods and shackled. Its final report, released on 17 November 2017 by commissioners Margaret White and Mick Gooda, found children had been subjected to 'regular, repeated and distressing mistreatment in detention' and that the law was often not followed, and recommended closing Don Dale, raising the age of criminal responsibility to 12 and not detaining children under 14.

n: Lumos — 'Funding Haitian Orphanages at the Cost of Children's Rights'
who: Mostly privately run, foreign-funded orphanages in Haiti; donors 92% from the US and 90% faith-based
d: Lumos researched Haiti's orphanages from October 2016 to February 2017, including a 2016 evaluation of 140 children in four orphanages with the government agency IBESR, and published its report in June 2017. It found at least US$70 million a year going to about a third of orphanages, with total funding estimated above $100 million a year; only 15% of orphanages were registered and at least 140 had conditions putting children at severe risk. It documented violence and severe neglect and, in a few cases, sexual abuse, trafficking and avoidable deaths, and evidence of orphanages recruiting children away from families — an 'orphanage business' it describes as increasingly recognised as trafficking.

n: Hogar Seguro Virgen de la Asunción — abuse, trafficking alerts and fire killing 41 girls
who: State-run children's home under the Secretariat of Social Welfare (SBS); National Civil Police
cover: Officials ignored repeated complaints: in November 2016 the Human Rights Ombudsman asked the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights for precautionary measures citing mistreatment and a trafficking network recruiting children from the home. On the day of the fire police guarding the locked room did not let the girls out.
d: About 700 children lived at the state home, built for a maximum of 500; most had committed no crime. Months before the fire prosecutors had recommended closing it over abuse allegations, and girls had protested overcrowding and alleged sexual abuse by staff. After an escape on 7 March 2017, police returned a group of girls and locked them in a room; on 8 March one girl set a mattress alight, killing 41 girls and injuring 15. The social welfare secretary, his deputy and the home's director were sacked and later charged. On 12 Aug 2025 a judge convicted six former officials of offences from manslaughter to abuse of authority, with sentences of 6 to 25 years; former secretary Carlos Rodas received 25 years and a police officer who held the key 13 years. The judge said the fire was the culmination of reported abuses not acted on, and ordered an investigation of former President Jimmy Morales.

n: Élan School, Poland, Maine — troubled-teen programme
who: Élan School (private behaviour-modification boarding school; NATSAP member)
cover: In the late 1970s staff refused a sheriff's lieutenant entry past the lobby after rumours of abuse.
d: Élan operated from 1970 until 1 April 2011, when it closed after decades of abuse reports from former students. Illinois officials removed eleven children in 1975 alleging mistreatment, and in 2007 New York education officials, who paid tuition for special-education students, alleged students were made to restrain peers and were sleep-deprived. The New Yorker (2000) and Time (2011) described 'the ring', in which students were made to fight one another. Maine State Police reopened the 1982 death of a 15-year-old student in 2016 but filed no charges. The record of sexual abuse rests on former students' accounts; no official sexual-abuse finding was located.

n: Scouts Canada — KPMG review of unreported abuse
who: Scouts Canada
cover: A 2011 CBC investigation found Scouts Canada had signed confidentiality agreements with more than a dozen abuse victims; KPMG found abusers had in some cases been 'removed discreetly' and records were inconsistent and poorly kept.
d: After a CBC investigation in autumn 2011 found confidentiality agreements that kept victims from speaking, Scouts Canada apologised and asked KPMG to audit 64 years of records. The review, released in 2012, examined 468 files and found the organisation failed at least 65 times to report sexual misconduct allegations to authorities, 13 of them after 1992 when reporting became mandatory. Scouts Canada then gave police all records it could find. In 1979 the Boy Scouts of America had sent a known abuser back to Canada without warning Scouts Canada; he was convicted in Victoria, BC in 1996 of assaulting four boys.

n: Moldova — children leaving residential institutions targeted by traffickers
who: Moldovan state residential institutions and boarding schools (Ministry of Education, Health, Labour)
d: Moldova had 68 residential institutions for children in the mid-2000s; children left them at 15–16 with no support beyond about US$70 and no follow-up. UNICEF reported that research showed institutionalised children were several times more vulnerable to trafficking than other children and that 'they often become easy prey for traffickers'. The US State Department's March 2007 human rights report said women and children were trafficked for sexual exploitation to Russia, Turkey, Israel, the UAE and other countries, and that 12% of trafficking victims assisted by IOM were minors.

n: 'Hidden in Plain Sight' — Australian Parliament recognises orphanage trafficking as modern slavery
place: Canberra (Joint Standing Committee on Foreign Affairs, Defence and Trade)
who: Australian volunteers, donors, schools and tour operators supporting overseas orphanages
d: The Joint Standing Committee's report 'Hidden in Plain Sight', released on 6 December 2017 from its inquiry into establishing a Modern Slavery Act, recognised orphanage trafficking as a form of modern slavery to be covered by the Act. A chapter was devoted to orphanage trafficking, orphanage tourism and Australian donations, with evidence from ReThink Orphanages, Lumos, the ChildSafe campaign and others. Australia's Modern Slavery Act followed in 2018; Lumos supported the change.

n: Colombia — ICBF investigation of 21 substitute (foster) homes
place: Colombia (Soacha, Antioquia, Bogotá, Meta and other departments)
who: Instituto Colombiano de Bienestar Familiar (ICBF) substitute-home (hogar sustituto) programme
d: In March 2018 the ICBF opened 21 investigations into foster homes nationwide for alleged verbal abuse, poor food and neglect and relocated 44 children and 14 adolescents, with about 3,100 homes still to review. The review followed a case in Soacha in which a man was jailed on charges of sexually abusing two girls aged 7 and 8 who were in ICBF custody in a foster home; he did not accept the charges.

n: Gwangju Inhwa School for the deaf — the 'Dogani' case
who: Gwangju Inhwa School for deaf students (founded 1961; principal was the founder's son)
cover: The teacher who alerted human rights groups in 2005 was fired; police acted only four months later after former students went to national TV; the city government and school board passed the case back and forth; appeal courts cut sentences to probation and four of the six teachers were reinstated.
d: A 2005 investigation found that six people at the school, including the headmaster, had sexually harassed or raped at least nine deaf students from 2000 onward. Four received prison terms, two of which were later suspended; two escaped punishment because the statute of limitations had expired. After the 2011 film 'Silenced' (Dogani), police opened a new investigation, the city moved to close the school in November 2011, and on 28 Oct 2011 the National Assembly passed the 'Dogani Law' removing the statute of limitations for sex crimes against children under 13 and disabled people. In July 2012 a former administrator was sentenced to 12 years for sexually assaulting an 18-year-old student in April 2005.

n: West Africa 'sex for aid' — UNHCR/Save the Children report and OIOS investigation
place: Refugee camps, Guéckédou area (Guinea), Liberia and Sierra Leone
who: Aid workers (UN agencies, national and international NGOs), peacekeepers and community leaders
d: A joint UNHCR and Save the Children UK mission reported in early 2002 that refugee children in Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone were being sexually exploited by employees of NGOs, UNHCR and other UN bodies, and by peacekeepers, often in exchange for food and aid. The UN Office of Internal Oversight Services then fully investigated 43 cases and substantiated 10, including the rape of a 14-year-old refugee girl in a Guinean camp and a UN Volunteer's sexual relationship with a girl of about 15 in Guéckédou; one substantiated case involved a peacekeeper, who was repatriated. OIOS (October 2002) found no allegation against a UN staff member substantiated and said it found no evidence of 'widespread' abuse; Save the Children UK replied that nothing the UN found made it think it was wrong.

n: MINUSCA Burundian and Gabonese contingents — Dékoa allegations
who: UN Multidimensional Integrated Stabilization Mission in CAR (MINUSCA) military contingents from Burundi and Gabon
d: The Secretary-General's 2017 report states that two allegations recorded in MINUSCA, concerning incidents in Dékoa and military personnel from Gabon and Burundi, led to interviews of some 136 alleged victims and accounted for 48% of all victims recorded in 2016. Investigations by the troop-contributing countries were still pending. Press accounts reported that at least 98 girls described abuse and 41 troops were identified and sent home without charges.

n: Bosnia — trafficking of women and girls; IPTF monitors and SFOR/DynCorp contractors
place: Prijedor, Bijeljina, Tuzla, Arizona Market (Brčko) and other towns
who: Traffickers and bar owners; local Bosnian police; UN International Police Task Force (IPTF) monitors; US SFOR civilian contractors (DynCorp)
cover: Immunity: IPTF monitors were repatriated rather than prosecuted (18 returned home; HRW found no prosecution by Nov 2002); DynCorp contractors were sent home, preventing their use as witnesses; DynCorp fired whistleblower Kathryn Bolkovac in April 2001.
d: Human Rights Watch's November 2002 report 'Hopes Betrayed' documented women and girls trafficked mostly from Moldova, Romania and Ukraine into post-war Bosnia and held in debt bondage in bars and brothels. Local police were found acting as owners, guards and clients; 18 IPTF monitors who purchased women, visited brothels or faced trafficking-related charges went home, and none was confirmed prosecuted. A US Army CID report documented DynCorp contractors buying women from brothels; one confessed to buying a woman (with an Uzi) for 1,600 Deutschmarks. On 2 August 2002 a British employment tribunal unanimously found DynCorp had unfairly dismissed IPTF monitor Kathryn Bolkovac after she reported the trafficking.

n: Oxfam GB in Haiti — 2011 investigation; possible involvement of minors not pursued
who: Oxfam GB staff in the 2010 earthquake response, including the country director
cover: Staff including the Belgian country director were allowed to resign; Oxfam did not report the allegations of abuse of minors to the Charity Commission or police in 2011.
d: Oxfam GB's 2011 internal investigation found staff in Haiti had used prostitutes, some of whom were alleged to be 'underage'. The Charity Commission's June 2019 inquiry found that not all lines of enquiry about minors were pursued and that Oxfam did not adequately investigate allegations in an email of 18 July 2011 that minors were being sexually abused by Oxfam employees, nor report them to the Commission or law enforcement. The Commission said it was no longer possible to conclude with certainty whether minors were involved or at risk.

n: Myanmar — Tatmadaw sexual violence against Rohingya and ethnic minority women, girls and boys (UN FFM)
place: Northern Rakhine (e.g. Min Gyi/Tula Toli), Kachin and Shan
who: Myanmar armed forces (Tatmadaw)
d: The Independent International Fact-Finding Mission on Myanmar found in 2018 that hundreds of Rohingya women and girls were raped during the 2017 'clearance operations', 80% of corroborated cases being gang rapes, and its August 2019 report found sexual and gender-based violence a 'hallmark' of Tatmadaw operations in Rakhine, Kachin and Shan. It documented Rohingya men and boys, some as young as twelve, detained at Buthidaung prison in 2012 and subjected to sexual violence.

n: Okinawa — rape of a 12-year-old girl by three US servicemen (1995)
who: US Navy and Marine Corps personnel from Camp Hansen
d: In September 1995 three US servicemen based on Okinawa abducted and raped a 12-year-old Okinawan schoolgirl. They were tried in a Japanese court and in 1996 were each found guilty and sentenced to between six years and six months and seven years in prison. The case triggered mass protests against the US bases.

n: Chibok schoolgirls abduction — Boko Haram
place: Government Girls Secondary School, Chibok, Borno
who: Boko Haram (JAS)
d: On the night of 14 April 2014 Boko Haram gunmen raided the dormitories of the Government Girls Secondary School in Chibok, Borno state, and loaded 276 girls onto trucks; more than 50 escaped within hours, mostly by jumping off the lorries, leaving 219 in captivity, some later found in the Sambisa Forest. Amnesty International said on the tenth anniversary in April 2024 that 82 girls remained in captivity and that 20 released girls had been forced to marry former Boko Haram fighters; in April 2015 it estimated that at least 2,000 women and girls had been abducted by the group since the start of 2014.

n: Lord's Resistance Army — child abduction and sexual slavery; ICC conviction of Dominic Ongwen
place: Northern Uganda (Acholiland: Gulu, Lukodi, Pajule, Odek, Abok)
who: Lord's Resistance Army (LRA), leader Joseph Kony (ICC warrant outstanding)
d: The LRA abducted tens of thousands of children in northern Uganda for use as fighters, porters and 'wives'; UNICEF estimated at least 25,000 by 2006. On 4 February 2021 ICC Trial Chamber IX convicted Sinia Brigade commander Dominic Ongwen, himself abducted as a child, of 61 crimes including rape, sexual slavery, forced marriage, forced pregnancy and the conscription and use of children under 15 (2002–2005); he was sentenced to 25 years on 6 May 2021, confirmed on appeal 15 December 2022. From 2008 the LRA abducted thousands more in DR Congo, South Sudan and CAR.

n: Somalia — Al-Shabaab abduction and sexual violence against children (UN verified 2024)
who: Al-Shabaab; also Somali National Army, police, Ethiopian Liyu Police, clan militias
d: The UN verified the abduction of 887 children in Somalia in 2024, 850 by Al-Shabaab, mainly for recruitment. It verified sexual violence against 267 children (265 girls): Al-Shabaab 120, unidentified 110, government security forces 14 (Somali National Army 11), Ethiopian Liyu Police 7. The Secretary-General noted a fivefold increase in gang rapes.

n: South Sudan — sexual violence against girls by SSPDF and other forces (UN verified)
who: South Sudan People's Defence Forces (SSPDF), SPLM/A-IO factions, police
d: The UN verified sexual violence against 94 girls, as young as 7, in South Sudan in 2022, 74 of them by the South Sudan People's Defence Forces, plus SPLM/A-IO Kit-Gwang (10), SPLM/A-IO (4) and the National Police Service (2). In 2024 it verified sexual violence against 7 girls, 5 by the SSPDF.

n: Cameroon — sexual violence against girls by armed forces and JAS (UN verified 2023)
who: Cameroon Armed Forces; JAS; unidentified perpetrators
d: The UN verified sexual violence against 17 girls in Cameroon in 2023, 10 attributed to the Cameroon Armed Forces, 6 to unidentified perpetrators and 1 to JAS. In 2024 it verified sexual violence against 6 girls (1 by the armed forces) and the abduction of 50 children.

n: Myanmar — abduction of children by armed forces and armed groups (UN verified)
who: Myanmar armed forces and Pyu Saw Htee; KIA; MNDAA; PDFs
d: The UN verified the abduction of 85 children in Myanmar in 2024, 41 by the Myanmar armed forces and affiliated militias and 33 by the KIA, mostly for recruitment; it verified the rape of 2 girls (Myanmar armed forces 1, KIA 1).

n: Duplessis Orphans (Quebec) — healthy orphans falsely certified mentally ill and confined
place: Quebec psychiatric hospitals and orphanages (e.g. Mont-Providence, Montreal)
who: Government of Quebec under Maurice Duplessis; Catholic religious orders running orphanages and hospitals
cover: No criminal charges resulted from the 1990s complaints; the 2001 compensation excluded victims of sexual or other abuse.
d: Under Premier Maurice Duplessis, many poor or illegitimate children in Quebec who were not mentally ill were sent in the 1940s and 1950s to church-run psychiatric institutions so that the orphanages could qualify for extra federal aid; Wikipedia, citing historians, gives subsidies of $2.75 a day for psychiatric patients against $1.25 for orphans. Survivors say they were beaten, sexually abused, and subjected to electroshock and lobotomies. Premier Lucien Bouchard apologised in 1999. In July 2001 the orphans accepted Quebec's final offer of $10,000 per person plus $1,000 for each year of wrongful confinement, about $25,000 each, not covering sexual or other abuse; about 3,000 were then still alive. Claims linking the orphans to CIA MKUltra experiments are not established by the sources consulted.

n: South Sudan — 'sex for aid' allegations against aid workers, Malakal UN Protection of Civilians site
place: Malakal Protection of Civilians site, Upper Nile
who: Staff named from IOM, MSF, WFP, World Vision and others in a UN-run camp
d: A September 2022 investigation by The New Humanitarian and Al Jazeera reported that between 2015 and 2022 aid workers in the UN-run Malakal Protection of Civilians site exploited displaced women and girls, including 'sex for aid'; women and girls reported being raped and becoming pregnant. Staff of IOM, MSF, WFP and World Vision were among those named.

n: Epstein — 2007 federal non-prosecution agreement and 2008 state plea
who: Jeffrey Epstein; US Attorney's Office, Southern District of Florida (Alexander Acosta)
cover: Lenient deal: the federal non-prosecution agreement (2007) dropped federal charges against Epstein and 'several suspected co-conspirators' in return for a state guilty plea; it was kept from victims. Epstein served 13 months of an 18-month term, much of it on daily work release. In Feb 2019 Judge Kenneth Marra ruled prosecutors violated the Crime Victims' Rights Act by not telling victims while urging them to 'have patience'. DOJ OPR (Nov 2020) found Acosta used 'poor judgment' but committed no professional misconduct; an 11-month gap in Acosta's incoming emails was noted.
d: After the FBI opened a federal probe, US Attorney Alexander Acosta's office negotiated a non-prosecution agreement in 2007. On 30 June 2008 Epstein pleaded guilty in Palm Beach County to soliciting prostitution and soliciting a minor; he was sentenced to 18 months, registered as a sex offender and was released on 22 July 2009 after 13 months. A 2018 Miami Herald series (Julie K. Brown) identified 80 victims and reopened scrutiny. Acosta resigned as US Labor Secretary in July 2019.

n: US Virgin Islands government suits — Epstein estate and JPMorgan
place: Little St. James, US Virgin Islands
who: Epstein estate; JPMorgan Chase; Deutsche Bank
cover: Banks were alleged to have facilitated and concealed the operation by keeping Epstein as a client. New York's financial regulator fined Deutsche Bank $150m in July 2020 for ignoring red flags on Epstein. UK regulators permanently banned former JPMorgan banker Jes Staley (upheld June 2025) for recklessly misleading them about his Epstein relationship.
d: Epstein owned the private island of Little St. James in the US Virgin Islands. The territory's government reached a $105m settlement with Epstein's estate and a $62.5m settlement with billionaire Leon Black. In December 2022 it sued JPMorgan Chase, claiming the bank ignored warning signs and facilitated Epstein's activities; JPMorgan agreed in June 2023 to pay $290m to nearly 200 Epstein victims in a class action and in September 2023 to pay the Virgin Islands $75m. The settlements carried no criminal findings.

n: Thorbjørn Jagland — charged with aggravated corruption over Epstein ties
who: Thorbjørn Jagland (former Norwegian PM, Council of Europe Secretary General, Nobel Committee chair)
d: After the US Justice Department's 2026 release of Epstein documents, Norway's economic-crime agency Økokrim opened an investigation into former prime minister and Council of Europe secretary-general Thorbjørn Jagland on suspicion of aggravated corruption, looking into 'whether gifts, travel and loans were received in connection with his position'. On 12 Feb 2026 his lawyers said he had been charged with aggravated corruption; his Oslo home and two other properties were searched. He denies all charges. This is a corruption case, not an abuse charge; recorded for the network's political reach.

n: Jimmy Savile — 'Giving Victims a Voice' (Met Police/NSPCC)
who: Jimmy Savile (BBC broadcaster); BBC; NHS hospitals; Metropolitan Police
cover: Earliest known police report dates from 1958, with police intelligence from 1963; Surrey Police investigated in 2007–09 without charges. A BBC Newsnight investigation was shelved in December 2011; the Pollard Review called the decision flawed.
d: After Savile's death in October 2011, an ITV documentary, 'Exposure: The Other Side of Jimmy Savile', broadcast on 3 Oct 2012, carried accounts of abuse of under-age teenage girls. The Metropolitan Police opened a criminal investigation, Operation Yewtree, on 19 Oct 2012. The January 2013 Met/NSPCC report 'Giving Victims a Voice' recorded 214 crimes across 28 police force areas, including 34 rape or penetration offences, from 1955 to 2009; 450 people had made allegations against him, 73% of them under 18 at the time. The CPS apologised for missing the chance to prosecute him in 2009. The report found no clear evidence that he operated in a paedophile ring.

n: Elm Guest House, London — VIP-abuse claims
who: Elm Guest House; Metropolitan Police (Operation Fernbridge)
d: Police placed the guest house near Barnes Common under surveillance from late 1981 after concerns about a 10-year-old boy there, raided it on 19 June 1982 and arrested 20 people; the owners were convicted of running a disorderly house. Claims spread in later decades that politicians and other prominent people attended abuse parties there. Giving evidence to IICSA on 7 March 2019, Met Commander Neil Jerome said police had found evidence of abuse of only one child, the 10-year-old boy, whose account and a medical examination showed he had been extensively abused; no prominent or well-known person was seen during surveillance or found in the raid; an IOPC investigation found 'no substance' in the claim that the boy named an 'Uncle Leon'; and the online 'Elm Guest House list' had 'zero evidential value'. The abuse of the boy occurred; the VIP claims are unsupported.

n: Operation Yewtree — post-Savile investigation of public figures
who: Metropolitan Police
d: Launched by the Metropolitan Police on 19 Oct 2012 after the Savile revelations, Yewtree had arrested 19 people by October 2015. Those convicted include Paul Gadd (Gary Glitter), Max Clifford, Rolf Harris, former DJ Chris Denning, Dave Lee Travis (one count, involving an adult) and, in April 2017, ex-BBC worker Geoffrey Wheeler, which the BBC called the operation's sixth conviction; Stoke Mandeville doctor Michael Salmon was also convicted in 2015 after a Yewtree investigation. Others were acquitted or never charged, including several well-known names, and must not be described as offenders.

n: Dutroux 'X-dossiers' — witness claims of an elite abuse network
who: Witnesses X1–X4 (claims); Belgian prosecutors
d: Witnesses told investigators in 1996–97 of abuse parties and unsolved murders involving Marc Dutroux, Michel Nihoul and prominent people. Prosecutors ultimately dismissed the statements, and investigators were criticised for leading a key witness; an officer charged in 1997 with falsifying her statements was cleared in 1999. In 1999 the Guardian reported renewed cover-up claims, and that the parliamentary inquiry's chair said his findings had been muzzled. The claims of an elite network remain unproven; a 1999 book by three journalists argued the witnesses were more credible than portrayed.

n: Hungary — presidential pardon in Bicske children's-home cover-up case
who: President Katalin Novák; Justice Minister Judit Varga; Bicske children's home
cover: In April 2023 the president pardoned the home's former deputy director, Endre Kónya, who had been convicted of helping cover up the director's sexual abuse of children.
d: In April 2023, ahead of a papal visit, President Katalin Novák pardoned about two dozen people, among them the former deputy director of the Bicske children's home, who had been sentenced in 2022 to three years four months for helping the home's director cover up his sexual abuse of children. The pardon became public in early February 2024 (reported by Telex on 2 Feb). After protests, Novák resigned on 10 Feb 2024, saying she had made a mistake; former justice minister Judit Varga, who countersigned the pardon, announced the same day that she was leaving public life. Prime Minister Orbán proposed a constitutional amendment barring pardons for crimes against children.

n: Lydia Cacho's arrest — Puebla governor and businessman protected exploitation ring
who: Mario Marín (Governor of Puebla); Kamel Nacif Borge (businessman)
cover: Intimidation of a journalist: after Cacho exposed the Cancún ring, Puebla police arrested her in Cancún and drove her about 900 miles to Puebla. Leaked calls (La Jornada, 14 Feb 2006) recorded Nacif and Marín discussing jailing her as a favour and having her abused in jail. Mexico's Supreme Court ruled 6–4 on 29 Nov 2007 that Marín had no case to answer.
d: After journalist Lydia Cacho's book 'Los demonios del Edén' (2005) linked Cancún businessman Jean Succar Kuri's child-exploitation network to Puebla businessman Kamel Nacif and Puebla governor Mario Marín, Cacho was arrested in 2005 and says she was tortured. Arrest warrants for torture were issued against Marín and Nacif; Marín was arrested in Acapulco in February 2021, and Nacif was detained in Lebanon in May 2021 and later released there. Marín was moved to house arrest in August 2024, returned to prison in April 2025, and in July 2026 was again granted house arrest on health and age grounds while his trial for alleged torture of Cacho continues. Neither has been convicted; both are accused of torture, not of the abuse itself.

n: Mark Foley — messages to congressional pages; House leadership 'negligent'
who: Rep. Mark Foley; House Republican leadership
cover: Complaints reached House staff and leaders around 2000–2005. The House Ethics Committee (Dec 2006) found Speaker Hastert and other leaders 'negligent' but recommended no sanctions. Florida's FDLE closed its probe in 2008 citing insufficient evidence and said Congress and Foley denied it access to data.
d: In late September 2006 sexually suggestive emails and instant messages from Rep. Mark Foley to teenage boys who had served as House pages became public; he resigned on 29 Sept 2006. On 8 Dec 2006 the House Ethics Committee found Republican members and staff had been negligent in handling earlier warnings about his conduct but that no House rules were broken, and recommended no punishment. No criminal charges were brought; Florida's state investigation was closed in September 2008 citing insufficient evidence.

n: USA Swimming — coaches banned for abuse; claims mishandled
who: USA Swimming
d: USA Swimming banned prominent coach Rick Curl for life in September 2012; a former swimmer said he had abused her from age 12 in 1983–1986. A February 2018 Orange County Register investigation reported that hundreds of swimmers were sexually abused over decades and that people in charge knew and ignored it, and that USA Swimming had banned 138 coaches and officials for life for sexual abuse and misconduct. Former coach Andy King, reported to Pacific Swimming officials in 2003, was arrested in 2009 and sentenced to 40 years after pleading no contest to 20 counts of felony child molestation, some victims as young as 10.

n: Johnny Kitagawa — Johnny & Associates talent agency
who: Johnny Kitagawa (founder, Johnny & Associates; now Smile-Up)
cover: Media silence: Shukan Bunshun's 2001 reports were upheld on the sexual allegations by the courts (damages reduced 2003; Supreme Court rejected appeal 2004), yet Japanese media barely covered them; journalists attributed this to the agency's power over talent bookings. Earliest cited report: Weekly Sankei, 1965.
d: An external investigation set up by Johnny & Associates concluded on 29 Aug 2023 that founder Johnny Kitagawa had sexually abused minors aspiring to be pop singers for decades; the BBC summarises the finding as abuse of hundreds of boys and young men over a six-decade career. The company admitted the abuse in September 2023, split into a new talent agency (Starto Entertainment) and Smile-Up, which handles compensation through a relief committee of three former judges. The BBC documentary 'Predator' (March 2023) and a former trainee's public allegations in April 2023 triggered the reckoning. In March 2024 Smile-Up's CEO told the BBC he believed two more perpetrators had worked at the agency. Kitagawa died in 2019 and was never charged.

n: Geelong Grammar School — Royal Commission case study 32
who: Geelong Grammar School (Anglican)
cover: The Royal Commission found the school repeatedly failed to investigate or report credible allegations, particularly under principal John Lewis (1980–94), and 'placed its own interests ahead of those of victims'. A 2007 settlement with victims of a boarding-house assistant was minuted as 'a very satisfactory financial outcome for the school'.
d: The Royal Commission's Case Study 32 heard from 13 former students who said they were abused by staff between 1956 and 1989. Five staff members were convicted of child sex offences against Geelong Grammar students, including a live-in boarding-house assistant who pleaded guilty in April 2005 to 41 counts of gross indecency and indecent acts and was convicted of offences against 40 students between 1985 and 1995 (six and a half years' jail), and a teacher convicted in 2008 over a 2007 offence. The report was published in December 2016.

n: Whyte Review — British Gymnastics
who: British Gymnastics
d: Anne Whyte QC's independent review of British Gymnastics, published in June 2022 and covering August 2008 to August 2020, received more than 400 submissions (133 from current and former gymnasts) and conducted 190 interviews. More than 40% of submissions described physical abuse by coaches and more than 50% emotional abuse; more than 25% referred to excessive weight management; some 30 submissions included allegations of sexual abuse, such as sexual assault, inappropriate touching and kissing as a punishment.

n: Maine Attorney General — Diocese of Portland (2004)
who: Catholic Diocese of Portland (Maine)
cover: Church officials kept abuse complaints secret and reassigned at least seven accused priests to parishes; one was later accused of abusing at least 10 girls
d: In February 2004 the Maine Attorney General reported on allegations reaching back 75 years against 63 men: diocesan priests, members of religious orders and church or school employees. The report found that church officials kept abuse charges secret and reassigned some accused priests, placing children at risk. No accusations of abuse after 1996 were found, and no one could be charged because of the statute of limitations.

n: Colorado Attorney General special master — three Catholic dioceses (2019)
who: Archdiocese of Denver; Dioceses of Colorado Springs and Pueblo
cover: On average 19.5 years passed between a credible allegation and restricting the priest; more than half of victims were abused after the diocese already knew the priest was an abuser; euphemisms used in records
d: A report by special master Bob Troyer, a former US Attorney appointed by Attorney General Phil Weiser, was released on 23 October 2019. It found that 43 priests sexually abused at least 166 children in Colorado's three Catholic dioceses over about 70 years, the most recent reported case in 1998. On average it took 19.5 years from a credible allegation to a restriction on the priest, and more than half the victims were abused after the church already knew of the priest. A supplemental report followed on 1 December 2020.

n: Nebraska Attorney General — three Catholic dioceses (2021)
who: Archdiocese of Omaha; Dioceses of Lincoln and Grand Island
cover: The church knew of the assaults and did not properly report them to law enforcement
d: The Nebraska Attorney General's Office released a report on 4 November 2021 after a three-year investigation of the state's three Catholic dioceses. It identified 258 victims, nearly 60% of them minors at the time, and 57 abusers, with abuse dating back to the 1930s. It found that the church knew of assaults and failed to report them properly to law enforcement. No charges were possible because the statute of limitations had expired.

n: Michigan Attorney General — diocese-by-diocese reports (2022–2026)
who: Catholic Dioceses of Marquette, Gaylord, Kalamazoo, Lansing, Grand Rapids and Saginaw (Archdiocese of Detroit pending)
d: After search warrants were executed at all seven Michigan dioceses in October 2018, the Attorney General's office published one report per diocese: Marquette (27 October 2022), Gaylord (8 January 2024), Kalamazoo (22 May 2024), Lansing (16 December 2024, 56 people accused, 48 of them priests), Grand Rapids (15 December 2025, 51 priests) and Saginaw (25 June 2026, 37 priests and one deacon). By June 2026 the investigation had received 1,276 tips, brought 11 criminal cases and obtained 9 convictions covering 38 survivors. The office states that inclusion in a report does not mean an allegation was substantiated.

n: Ramsey County v. Archdiocese of St. Paul and Minneapolis (2015–2016)
who: Catholic Archdiocese of St. Paul and Minneapolis
cover: The archdiocese admitted it 'failed to adequately respond and prevent the sexual abuse' of three boys by a priest
d: In June 2015 the Ramsey County Attorney filed six gross misdemeanor child endangerment charges against the archdiocese itself over its handling of priest Curtis Wehmeyer, later imprisoned for abusing three brothers. The charges were dropped on 20 July 2016 after the archdiocese admitted in court papers that it had failed to adequately respond to and prevent the abuse. A December 2015 civil settlement placed the archdiocese under court oversight until February 2020.

n: Justice Department inspector general — FBI mishandling of Nassar allegations (2021)
who: FBI Indianapolis field office; USA Gymnastics
cover: FBI Indianapolis officials took months to open a formal investigation, interviewed only one of three athletes (by phone), and later gave incomplete and inaccurate information to internal FBI inquiries
d: The Justice Department's Office of the Inspector General reported on 14 July 2021 that the FBI made 'numerous and fundamental errors' after USA Gymnastics reported allegations against Larry Nassar to its Indianapolis office in 2015. Months passed before a formal investigation was opened; agents interviewed only one of three athletes, by phone. Officials later gave incomplete and inaccurate information when their handling was questioned. At least 40 girls and women reported being abused during the 14 months the FBI knew of the allegations.

n: Texas Youth Commission sexual abuse scandal — Rangers report and legislative takeover (2007)
place: West Texas State School, Pyote, Texas
who: Texas Youth Commission (state juvenile corrections)
cover: Complaints at the West Texas State School from 2001 to 2005 were largely ignored; a TYC headquarters inquiry found no abuse; the local district attorney never took the Texas Rangers' case to a grand jury
d: A Texas Ranger's 229-page report documented sexual abuse of boys by two senior administrators at the West Texas State School in Pyote, where complaints from 2001 to 2005 had been largely ignored and the local prosecutor did not take the case to a grand jury; the two were indicted in April 2007. When this became public in February 2007, investigators counted more than 750 sexual abuse complaints across all 13 Texas Youth Commission facilities from January 2000 to February 2007. The TYC board resigned on 16 March 2007, the legislature approved a conservator for the agency, and by May 2007, 93 employees had been suspended, fired or forced to retire.

n: Quebec National Assembly special commission on the sexual exploitation of minors (2020)
who: Pimping networks and sex-trade establishments exploiting minors in Quebec
d: A cross-party special commission of Quebec's National Assembly studied the sexual exploitation of minors for 18 months, with hearings in Quebec City, Montreal and Val-d'Or, and tabled its final report on 3 December 2020. It estimated about 600 establishments in Quebec, such as strip clubs, massage parlours and escort agencies, where a man could find a teenager for sex, described Montreal as a national hub, and said pimps could earn up to $300,000 a year. It made 58 recommendations, the first being to make the fight against sexual exploitation of minors a national priority.

n: Senate 'Forgotten Australians' — children in institutional care (2004)
who: Australian orphanages, children's homes, foster care and other out-of-home care run by states, churches and charities
d: The Senate Community Affairs References Committee tabled 'Forgotten Australians: A report on Australians who experienced institutional or out-of-home care as children' on 30 August 2004. It received 614 submissions and estimated that about 500,000 people had been placed in institutions or foster care, and heard accounts of neglect, beatings, psychological cruelty, forced labour and sexual assault and rape by carers, other children, visitors and foster families. Prime Minister Kevin Rudd apologised in Parliament to Forgotten Australians and former child migrants on 16 November 2009.

n: Nauru detention centre — Moss Review and Senate inquiry on abuse of asylum-seeker children (2015)
who: Australian-funded Regional Processing Centre on Nauru; contracted guards and staff
cover: Staff wrote in an open letter in April 2015 that the Australian government had known of alleged abuses against women and children for more than 18 months
d: The Moss Review, commissioned by the Australian government and published in March 2015, was aware of three rape allegations at the Australian-run Regional Processing Centre on Nauru, one involving a minor, confirmed that a guard demanded to see a female detainee naked in exchange for extra shower time with her young child, and concluded that guards trading marijuana with detainees for sexual favours was possibly occurring. In April 2015 staff alleged multiple instances of sexual abuse of women and children in an open letter. A Senate select committee reported on 31 August 2015 in 'Taking responsibility: conditions and circumstances at Australia's Regional Processing Centre in Nauru'.

n: Belgium — Chamber special committee on sexual abuse in the Church (Lalieux, 2011)
who: Catholic Church in Belgium; Belgian justice system
d: After the June 2010 police raids that ended the Adriaenssens commission, the Belgian Chamber set up a special committee on the handling of sexual abuse in relationships of authority, especially within the Church, chaired by Karine Lalieux. Its report, approved unanimously on 30 March 2011, found abuse in every sector of the church and across the country, especially in Catholic boarding schools, with families reporting at least 13 suicides. It recommended an independent arbitration body for compensation and extending the limitation period from 10 to 15 years after a victim turns 18. The arbitration centre and its compensation scheme followed in 2012.

n: Netherlands — De Vries Commission on sexual abuse in organised sport (2017)
who: Dutch sports clubs and federations; NOC*NSF
d: The Dutch Olympic Committee NOC*NSF set up a commission led by former minister Klaas de Vries in May 2017; it reported on 12 December 2017. A survey found about 12% of athletes had experienced sexually transgressive behaviour as children and about 4% sexual assault or rape. The commission analysed 686 cases reported between 2001 and 2017, in which 60% of victims were under 16 and 70% of perpetrators were coaches or supervisors, and received 103 new reports. It recommended a reporting duty for sports boards.

n: Germany — Federal Independent Commissioner (Bergmann) final report (2011)
who: Churches, schools, sports clubs, homes and families in Germany
d: After the 2010 revelations at Canisius-Kolleg and other schools, the federal government appointed former minister Christine Bergmann as Independent Commissioner. Her final report, presented on 24 May 2011 to the Round Table on Child Sexual Abuse, drew on about 13,000 letters and 2,000 phone calls from victims and relatives about abuse in churches, schools, sports clubs and families. It recommended that institutions where abuse occurred make one-time payments based on what courts would award, that therapy costs be covered, and that an independent body oversee implementation. A permanent federal commissioner's office followed, and in 2016 an Independent Commission for the investigation of child sexual abuse began work.

n: Germany — Bund der Pfadfinderinnen und Pfadfinder (BdP) study (2024)
who: Bund der Pfadfinderinnen und Pfadfinder (non-denominational scout association)
d: The BdP commissioned IPP Munich, working with the Dissens institute, to study sexualised violence in the association from its founding in 1976 to 2006. Presented on 29 February 2024, the study identified 103 victims (123 including cases that could not be dated or assigned) and 36 accused (50 with the same additions), almost all male; most incidents were in the 1980s and 1990s. It found two main perpetrator types, older adult leaders and adolescents or young adults who used leadership roles, and named weak oversight of young leaders, informal power imbalances, strong group loyalty and silence about sexuality as risk factors.

n: Germany — Archdiocese of Freiburg commission report (2023)
who: Catholic Archdiocese of Freiburg
cover: The report found that Archbishop Robert Zollitsch (from 2003) ignored canon law, did not report abuse suspicions to the Vatican although required from 2002, and that files were manipulated; Archbishop Oskar Saier (1978–2002) transferred offenders without informing parishes.
d: The archdiocese's independent reappraisal commission presented a roughly 600-page report on 18 April 2023, examining 24 cases in depth from 1945 onward. The commission chair, Magnus Striet, said more than 540 people were assumed to have been victims of more than 250 clerics; an earlier count had found at least 442 victims. It found that former archbishop Robert Zollitsch, who also chaired the German Bishops' Conference from 2008 to 2014, failed up to the point of deliberate concealment and ignored canon law, and that his predecessor Oskar Saier transferred offenders without informing parishes.

n: Germany — Archdiocese of Berlin, Redeker Sellner Dahs report (2021)
who: Catholic Archdiocese of Berlin
d: The law firm Redeker Sellner Dahs, commissioned by the Archdiocese of Berlin, presented its report in part on 29 January 2021, covering the period from 1946. It identified 61 accused clergy and at least 121 known victims. A part on the responsibility of named officials was kept back for data-protection reasons, reviewed by another firm and presented at the end of June 2021.

n: Italy — Il Forteto community, Tuscany: abuse of children placed by courts
who: Il Forteto agricultural cooperative and community; Tuscany Region, juvenile court and local authorities that placed and accredited it
cover: The founder already had a final conviction in 1985, yet courts and social services kept placing children there; parliament's 2024 commission is to establish why authorities kept accrediting the community after court rulings on sexual abuse and mistreatment.
d: Il Forteto, a cooperative and community at Vicchio in the Mugello near Florence, received children placed by juvenile courts and social services for decades. Its founder, Rodolfo Fiesoli, was definitively sentenced to 14 years and 10 months for abuse, although a conviction had already become final in 1985 and placements continued. Two Tuscan regional council inquiry commissions examined the case; a parliamentary inquiry in the previous legislature did not finish with a final report, and a new bicameral commission of inquiry was created by Law 47 of 25 March 2024 and installed on 1 August 2024. Its task is to establish institutional responsibilities and why authorities kept accrediting the community after court rulings on abuse and mistreatment.

n: Diocese of Würzburg — Schneider report for the review commission (2025)
who: Catholic Diocese of Würzburg (43 of 51 accused were clergy)
cover: Until the early 2000s some accused clergy received 'systematic protection'.
d: Lawyer Hendrik Schneider, commissioned by the diocese's independent review commission (UKAM), presented his report on 8 April 2025 covering 1949 to 2019. It counted 51 accused, 43 of them clergy, and 226 victims subject to 449 documented acts, which the report extrapolated to about 3,053 acts. The average age of victims at the first act was 9.8 years. It found systematic protection of some accused clergy until the early 2000s. Earlier, in 2019, lawyer Hans-Jochen Schrepfer reviewed nearly 3,000 personnel files, and the Würzburg law firm Cornea Franz reviewed the records of the diocese's three Kilianeen boys' boarding schools.

n: Diocese of Speyer — University of Mannheim study, part 1 (2025)
who: Catholic Diocese of Speyer; religious orders working in it
cover: Accused priests were either punished individually or protected; structural problems, including weak oversight of religious orders, were ignored.
d: Historian Sylvia Schraut of the University of Mannheim, in a study begun in April 2023 at the initiative of the diocese's independent review commission, presented part 1 on 8 May 2025. It identified 109 accused clergy since 1946, two-thirds born before 1920; half the offences took place in the 1950s and 1960s, in church homes, lessons, confession and parish work. The church either punished accused priests individually or shielded them, and oversight of religious orders was weak. Part 2, with case analyses, is due in 2027. Separately, in 2020 the Darmstadt social court granted victim compensation to a man abused in the former Niederbronn Sisters' children's home in Speyer; he said the nuns brought children to abusers, and he and two other men independently said a former vicar general abused them there between 1963 and 1975.

n: German Capuchin Province — Westpfahl Spilker Wastl report (2011)
who: Capuchin Order, German Province (former Bavarian and Rhine-Westphalian provinces); Burghausen seminary
cover: Files of deceased friars appear to have been purged; before 2009 no sanctions against suspects were found; no church-law preliminary investigation was opened in any case, and the reviewers found no evidence that the province passed reports to prosecutors.
d: Lawyer Martin Pusch of Westpfahl Spilker Wastl, commissioned by the German Capuchin Province, reported on 30 November 2011. He found 32 accused friars, 19 of them accused of sexual abuse and at least 11 believed to have abused minors, mostly in schools and training institutions including the Burghausen seminary; no criminal or church-court conviction was found in any case. Files of deceased friars appeared to have been purged, and no sanctions were found before 2009, when three suspects were suspended and one elderly friar transferred. No church-law investigation was opened in any case, and before 2010 victims received no response or support.

n: Aloisiuskolleg Bonn (Jesuit school) — Zinsmeister report (2011)
who: Society of Jesus — Aloisiuskolleg boarding school, Bonn
cover: A priest responsible for more than half the reports, later rector, was never stopped.
d: An independent team led by Cologne law professor Julia Zinsmeister presented its report on the Jesuit Aloisiuskolleg on 15 February 2011, covering about 60 years. It received 58 reports of abuse and other violations against 23 staff, 18 Jesuit priests and 5 lay employees, most active in the 1950s and 1960s. Ten cases concerned the former headmaster, who led and lived at the school from 1968 to 2008, and would count as sexual abuse under strict criminal-law standards. The authors blamed the order's closed organisational culture.

n: West German children's cure homes ('Verschickungskinder') — Humboldt University report (2025)
who: Children's cure homes run by welfare organisations, municipalities and private operators, financed by health and pension insurers; Deutsche Rentenversicherung, Caritas, Diakonie and German Red Cross
d: A Humboldt University team led by historian Alexander Nützenadel published the first nationwide report on West German children's cure homes on 15 May 2025, jointly with the German pension insurance (DRV), Caritas, Diakonie and the German Red Cross. It estimates that 11.4 million children stayed in such homes between 1951 and 1990 and describes humiliation, intimidation and violence as structural, caused by underfunding, staff shortages and inadequate supervision; many children faced physical, psychological and sexualised violence, though the study says no count is possible. No home was closed because of complaints. The four organisations expressed regret and accepted responsibility.

n: Diocese of Rottenburg-Stuttgart — diocesan abuse figures (2023)
who: Catholic Diocese of Rottenburg-Stuttgart — clergy, religious sisters and lay staff
d: The Diocese of Rottenburg-Stuttgart's third report on investigation and recognition, with figures as of 1 September 2023 and published in October 2023, counted 207 accused (114 priests, deacons and male religious with a diocesan contract, 17 other religious priests, 54 lay people and 21 religious sisters) and 421 known victims for 1946 to 2023. Cases are handled by the diocese's abuse commission (KsM), set up in 2002. The diocese's independent review commission, formed in December 2021, published its first report in February 2023.

n: SOS Children's Villages — Independent Special Commission (ISC) worldwide report (2023)
who: SOS Children's Villages (federation of member associations; International Senate); former senior staff
cover: Former senior staff in some member associations knew of abuse and failed to act or concealed reports; serious abuse was not reported to national authorities.
d: An Independent Special Commission appointed by the International Senate of SOS Children's Villages in 2021, chaired by former Kenyan Chief Justice Willy Mutunga with former Delhi High Court acting chief justice Gita Mittal, issued its summary report on 6 June 2023. Using a 'reasonable grounds to believe' standard, it confirmed serious allegations of child sexual and physical abuse in several member associations in Africa, Asia and Central America, and found cover-ups of past sexual abuse and failures to report to national authorities in more than one association. Countries named in the report include Nepal, Cambodia, India, Kenya, Panama, Sierra Leone and Syria. A confidential 991-page part two went to the organisation's Senate and Executive Board on 2 May 2023; in November 2025 SOS Children's Villages International said it was examining whether parts could be passed to prosecutors.

n: Society of Jesus in Spain — report on abuse since 1927 (2021)
who: Society of Jesus (Jesuits), Spain — 65 of the 96 accused abused children
d: In January 2021 the Jesuits in Spain published a report admitting 118 cases of sexual abuse since 1927, 81 of them against children and 37 against adults. It named 96 accused Jesuits, about 1.08% of members since 1927; of the 65 who abused children, 48 had died and 17 were alive. AP described it as the first comprehensive internal inquiry into abuse by a religious order in Spain. Victims' groups criticised it for not naming perpetrators or those who covered up abuse.

n: Belgian Chamber commission of inquiry on sexual abuse in the Church after 'Godvergeten' (2024)
who: Catholic Church in Belgium; Belgian justice system
cover: The commission noted 58% of cases are dismissed by prosecutors and called for a new inquiry into the 2010 'Operation Kelk' raids after the High Council of Justice reported dysfunctions.
d: The federal Chamber set up a parliamentary commission of inquiry into sexual abuse in the Church and elsewhere, chaired by Sophie De Wit (N-VA), after the 2023 VRT series 'Godvergeten'. Its final report of 2 May 2024 made 137 recommendations, including that the Church proactively trace perpetrators through its archives and give police and courts access to relevant church files, and a legal study on retroactively ending the limitation period for child sexual abuse. It called for reducing the 58% of sexual-violence cases dismissed by prosecutors, and for a new inquiry into the 2010 'Operation Kelk' investigation after the High Council of Justice reported dysfunctions. It proposed an abuse commissioner, a centre of expertise and an arbitration body for time-barred cases.

n: Slovakia — bishops' commission evaluation report on abuse 2018–2023 (2024)
who: Catholic Church in Slovakia — Latin dioceses, Greek Catholic eparchies and religious orders
d: The Slovak bishops' commission for the protection of minors published its 'Evaluation Report 2018–2023' in March 2024, the first such report in Slovakia, counting complaints from 1990 onward. Of 68 complaints, 39 were confirmed and closed, 17 remained open, 7 could not be resolved and 5 were not confirmed; the confirmed cases involved more than 44 victims. Fifty complaints concerned Latin-rite dioceses, three Greek Catholic eparchies and 15 religious orders.

n: UK cadet forces — 363 sexual abuse allegations in five years (BBC Panorama, MoD figures)
who: Army Cadet Force, Air Training Corps and Sea Cadets (sponsored by the Ministry of Defence)
cover: Former cadets and families told the BBC that officials discouraged them from going to the police.
d: A BBC Panorama investigation in July 2017, using Freedom of Information figures from the Ministry of Defence, found 363 allegations of sexual abuse across the army, air and sea cadet forces between 2012 and 2017, both current and historical. Of these, 282 were referred to police and 99 adult instructors were dismissed. The programme reported that the MoD had paid more than £2 million to victims and that some victims and families had been urged not to tell police. The MoD said it had robust procedures and encouraged victims to report to police.

n: United States — 4,556 sexual abuse complaints from unaccompanied migrant children in ORR shelters (2014-2018)
place: Washington, D.C. (Office of Refugee Resettlement, HHS)
who: Office of Refugee Resettlement (HHS) and contracted shelters for unaccompanied migrant children
d: HHS records released in February 2019 by Rep. Ted Deutch showed 4,556 complaints of sexual abuse reported to the Office of Refugee Resettlement by unaccompanied migrant children in its care between October 2014 and July 2018. The Justice Department received 1,303 such complaints in fiscal years 2015-2018, of which 178 involved adult staff at the facilities. HHS said the figures were mischaracterised and that none of the allegations involved federal ORR staff.

n: Anglican Church of Australia — Parkinson study of reported child sexual abuse, 17 dioceses (2009)
who: Anglican Church of Australia (17 of 23 dioceses)
d: The Anglican Church of Australia's Professional Standards Commission asked for this study after the 2004 General Synod; University of Sydney researchers Patrick Parkinson, Kim Oates and Amanda Jayakody published it in May 2009. It counted 191 cases of alleged child sexual abuse reported to 17 of the 23 dioceses between 1990 and 2008, made by 180 complainants against 135 people. Nearly two-thirds of the accused were clergy or candidates for ordination, about three-quarters of complainants were male, and on average 23 years passed between the abuse and the complaint. Eight percent of cases were never investigated; of 44 cases known to have gone to court, 53% ended in conviction.

n: South Yorkshire — Drew review of South Yorkshire Police's handling of child sexual exploitation (2016)
who: South Yorkshire Police
d: South Yorkshire's Police and Crime Commissioner, Alan Billings, commissioned Professor John Drew to review the force's handling of child sexual exploitation after concerns that Sheffield had seen failings similar to Rotherham's. The review, published on 23 March 2016, found the force had confronted 'a raft of weaknesses' in its earlier approach and had made strong progress over the previous three years. Drew said his picture was incomplete because he could not examine about 200 IPCC complaints about officers linked to Rotherham or speak to witnesses in ongoing criminal cases. The outgoing chief constable said the force had charged 124 people with child sexual exploitation offences since the 2014 Jay report.

n: IICSA — child sexual exploitation by organised networks (six areas, 2022)
place: England and Wales (St Helens, Tower Hamlets, Swansea, Durham, Bristol, Warwickshire)
who: Organised networks exploiting children; local authorities and police forces in six case-study areas
cover: Victims were sometimes treated as offenders while perpetrators were often not investigated or prosecuted.
d: IICSA's report of 1 February 2022 examined St Helens, Tower Hamlets, Swansea, Durham, Bristol and Warwickshire and found that network exploitation occurs in all parts of England and Wales and that councils and police showed extensive failures. Officials had wrongly assumed exploitation was declining; it had become more hidden, including through phones, apps and live-streaming for payment. None of the six areas recorded the ethnicity of victims or alleged perpetrators. It made six recommendations, including mandatory data collection.

n: Scottish Child Abuse Inquiry — Queen Victoria School, Dunblane (military boarding school)
who: Queen Victoria School (Ministry of Defence boarding school for children of service personnel)
d: The inquiry's thirteenth volume of findings, published 22 October 2024, found 'dreadful abuse' at Queen Victoria School, especially from the late 1950s to the early 1990s, with weak oversight and a military culture of silence. A teacher employed 1973–1993 groomed and sexually abused several primary-age boys and the school did not act on his well-known behaviour. A drumming instructor sexually abused seven female pupils between 2011 and 2019, after child protection systems were in place.

n: Catholic Church in Scotland — McLellan Commission (2015)
who: Catholic Church in Scotland (Bishops' Conference of Scotland)
cover: The report condemned a 'culture of secrecy and cover-up' that let abuse stay hidden.
d: At the invitation of the Bishops' Conference of Scotland, former Church of Scotland Moderator Andrew McLellan chaired a commission reviewing the Catholic Church's safeguarding policy and practice; its 99-page report was published on 18 August 2015. It called abuse 'the greatest challenge facing the whole Catholic Church in Scotland', condemned a 'culture of secrecy and cover-up', said the Church had not made significant structural changes, and made eight key recommendations. Archbishop Philip Tartaglia offered a 'profound apology' to victims.

n: Macur Review of the Waterhouse Inquiry (North Wales, 2016)
who: Waterhouse Inquiry (Lost in Care); North Wales children's homes
d: The UK government set up the Macur Review in 2012 to check whether the Waterhouse Inquiry into abuse in North Wales children's homes had been given all relevant material and had investigated within its terms. Lady Justice Macur reported in March 2016 and found no evidence of significant failings that would undermine Waterhouse's findings. She made six recommendations, the last advising caution about re-opening past inquiries.

n: UK government study of 'satanic ritual abuse' claims — La Fontaine report (1994)
who: Claims of organised satanic/ritual abuse made in 84 cases, including those that led to removals of children in Rochdale and Orkney
d: Health Secretary Virginia Bottomley commissioned anthropologist Jean La Fontaine in 1991 after children were removed from homes in Rochdale and Orkney on claims of ritual abuse. Her report, made public on 3 June 1994, examined 84 cases and found no evidence supporting any allegation of satanic abuse. Only three claims of 'ritual' abuse were substantiated, and she said even those did not merit that description.

n: CEOP thematic assessment 'Out of mind, out of sight' — localised grooming (2011)
who: Groups grooming children in person ('localised grooming'); Local Safeguarding Children Boards
