d: The Child Exploitation and Online Protection Centre announced in January 2011 a thematic assessment of 'localised grooming' and published 'Out of mind, out of sight' later that year. It recorded 2,379 offenders since the start of 2008, mostly men aged 18 to 24 (38% white, 26% Asian, 3% black, ethnicity unknown in 32%), with about 90% of victims white. It found about two-thirds of Local Safeguarding Children Boards were not meeting national guidance and that victims did not expect to be believed. CEOP warned the data were not comprehensive enough to draw firm conclusions.

n: Ofsted review of sexual abuse in schools and colleges (2021)
who: Schools and colleges in England (state and private)
d: After thousands of anonymous accounts were posted to the Everyone's Invited website, the government asked Ofsted to review sexual abuse in schools and colleges. Its report of 10 June 2021, based on visits to 32 state and private schools and colleges and talks with more than 900 young people, found sexual harassment had become normalised: 79% of girls said sexual assault of any kind happens 'a lot' or 'sometimes' between peers and 64% said so of unwanted touching. Many teachers underestimated the problem and pupils saw no point in reporting.

n: Ireland — Murphy inquiry into child sexual abuse in swimming (1998)
who: Irish Amateur Swimming Association (IASA); national coaches including Derry O'Rourke and George Gibney (Gibney never tried)
cover: The report found 'total systems failure' in the IASA; charges against another coach were dropped after a 1994 judicial review because of delay.
d: The Irish government asked senior counsel Roderick Murphy to inquire after former Olympic coach Derry O'Rourke was jailed for 12 years for abusing 11 girl swimmers. His 165-page report (1998) found that children had come to believe abuse was a normal part of their training, and a 'total systems failure' in the Irish Amateur Swimming Association. It noted Garda investigations into two other coaches and made more than 100 recommendations; the minister cut the association's funding.

n: Denmark — state investigation of abuse in special-care institutions 1933–1980 (særforsorgen)
place: Denmark (Ministry of Social Affairs; apology given at Horsens)
who: Danish state special-care institutions (særforsorgen) for children and adults with intellectual and physical disabilities
d: An investigation ordered by the Danish government in 2020, financed by the Ministry of Social Affairs and the Elderly and carried out by Danmarks Forsorgsmuseum (Svendborg Museum), was published in March 2022. It documented widespread abuse and neglect, including sexual assault, of children, young people and adults placed in state special-care institutions between 1933 and 1980, and found the state did not carry out systematic oversight. About 15,000 people with disabilities were committed. Social affairs minister Pernille Rosenkrantz-Theil gave an official apology on behalf of the state at Horsens on 11 September 2023.

n: Guatemala — Peace Archives report: army and state role in adoptions of children during the war (1977–1989)
place: Guatemala City (Secretaría de la Paz; Hogar Elisa Martínez)
who: Guatemalan armed forces and National Police; Secretaría de Bienestar Social (Hogar Elisa Martínez); notaries and courts
cover: Decree 54-77 (1977) let notaries complete adoptions without prior judicial approval; the welfare secretariat kept no record of how many children it received
d: In September 2009 the Dirección de los Archivos de la Paz, part of the Peace Secretariat of the Presidency set up under President Álvaro Colom, published a study of adoptions during the internal armed conflict. It reviewed 333 of 670 adoption files recorded for 1977–1989 and found that the army and National Police transported children into the adoption system, that adoptions often rested on court declarations of abandonment with little effort to find parents, and that a 1977 decree let notaries formalise adoptions without a judge. Chief investigator Marco Tulio Álvarez told the press the children went mainly to the United States, Sweden, Italy and France.

n: Nepal — National Human Rights Commission national reports on trafficking: an estimated 5,000 children trafficked in a year
who: Trafficking networks moving women and girls across the open border to India and on to third countries
d: Nepal's National Human Rights Commission, through its Office of the Special Rapporteur on Trafficking in Persons, has published national reports on trafficking since 2005. Its report released in August 2019 estimated that about 35,000 Nepalis were trafficked in 2018, including 5,000 children, and that nearly 1.5 million were at risk. It said nearly 1,000 Nepali women and girls are rescued from India each year and that poor screening at the open border makes cross-border trafficking hard to control. Its 2018 report said girls and women are trafficked to India for prostitution, orchestra dancing, circus work and marriage, and some are moved on to third countries.

n: Brazil — Joint Congressional Inquiry (CPMI) into networks sexually exploiting children (2004)
who: Networks including politicians, businessmen and clergy named by the commission
d: A joint commission of 11 senators and 11 deputies, created in 2003 to investigate violence and networks of sexual exploitation of children and adolescents, had by May 2004 received more than 800 complaints, heard more than 300 people and visited 14 states. Its final report, approved on 13 July 2004, put more than 250 people on notice, among them 20 serving politicians (including one federal deputy, two state deputies and three mayors), about 30 businessmen and five priests, and passed the cases to federal and state prosecutors. The commission's bill rewriting the Penal Code chapter on 'crimes against public morals' (PLS 253/2004) became Law 12.015 of 2009.

n: Chile — National Prosecutor's Office: 166 investigations of clergy and church workers, 248 victims (2019)
who: Catholic clergy, religious and lay church workers; 152 priests, 10 bishops, 9 deacons, 15 lay people and 27 non-clerical members of orders among those investigated
d: Chile's National Prosecutor's Office reviewed sexual abuse by members of the Catholic Church nationally. Its balance of 30 April 2019 counted 166 investigations and 221 people investigated (152 priests, 10 bishops, 9 deacons, 15 lay people and 27 non-clerical members of orders), and 248 victims, of whom 131 were children or adolescents, 35 adults and 82 not recorded. In July 2018 the office had already reported five cases of alleged cover-up or obstruction aimed at bishops or superiors of congregations.

n: Trinidad and Tobago — Sabga task force on children's homes, kept secret for 25 years
who: Children's homes incl. St Dominic's Children's Home and St Jude's School for Girls
cover: Abuser at St Dominic's was asked to resign and allegedly helped into hospital work; report never published by government
d: A task force appointed by the Cabinet in 1997 and chaired by Robert Sabga visited nine children's homes. It found that a male employee at St Dominic's Children's Home had repeatedly sexually abused some 30 to 40 children and, when discovered, was asked to resign and allegedly helped to find work at a hospital; it also recorded beatings at St Jude's School for Girls. The report was never published; the Trinidad Express published its findings in May 2022.

n: Special Court for Sierra Leone — Charles Taylor convicted of aiding sexual slavery and use of child soldiers (2012)
place: Freetown (Special Court; trial held in The Hague)
who: Charles Taylor, former President of Liberia; Revolutionary United Front (RUF) and allied rebel forces he aided
d: On 26 April 2012 the Special Court for Sierra Leone, sitting in The Hague, convicted former Liberian president Charles Taylor on all 11 counts of war crimes and crimes against humanity, on the basis of aiding and abetting crimes by the Revolutionary United Front during Sierra Leone's civil war, including sexual slavery and the recruitment and use of children under 15 as fighters. He was sentenced to 50 years in prison in May 2012.

n: South Sudan — UN Commission finds rape, abduction and sexual slavery of women and girls by armed forces and groups (2022)
who: South Sudan People's Defence Forces, opposition forces and armed groups; intercommunal militias
cover: Commission described impunity for armed forces in Western Equatoria; court-ordered compensation to victims in Yei unpaid
d: The UN Commission on Human Rights in South Sudan presented a report on conflict-related sexual violence to the Human Rights Council on 18 March 2022. It found that parties to the conflict used rape of women and girls as a weapon of terror and political repression, and that abductions of women and girls for forced marriage and sexual slavery had increased in Jonglei, the Greater Pibor Administrative Area, Warrap and Lakes. It noted that a military court in Yei had convicted SSPDF soldiers of rape in late 2020 but victims had not been paid court-ordered compensation.

n: Timor-Leste — Truth commission finds over 4,000 children taken to Indonesia, renamed and converted (2005)
who: Indonesian military; Islamic and other organisations and individuals that took children
d: The Commission for Reception, Truth and Reconciliation (CAVR) published its final report, Chega!, in 2005, covering 1974 to 1999. It found that at least 4,000 children were forcibly taken from their families and moved illegally to Indonesia during the occupation, by military units, some of which used them as child soldiers or servants, and by Islamic organisations that converted them; children were often renamed and lost contact with their families. It called separating a child from their true identity, culture, religion or language a grave breach of the Fourth Geneva Convention. CAVR and the joint Indonesia–Timor-Leste Commission of Truth and Friendship recommended a commission to search for the missing children, which was never created.

n: Playpen / Operation Pacifier — FBI ran the site for 13 days
place: North Carolina (sentencing court); operator from Florida
who: Playpen (Tor site; administrator Steven W. Chase, convicted)
cover: After seizing the server the FBI kept Playpen running from 19 February to 4 March 2015 under a court warrant and used malware (a 'Network Investigative Technique') to unmask users; the EFF criticised the operation as continued distribution, and the 11th Circuit (2019) held the warrant invalid but did not exclude the evidence (good-faith exception). In 2017 the FBI dropped charges against one defendant rather than disclose the NIT.
d: Playpen operated on Tor from August 2014 to March 2015 and had over 215,000 users (Europol: more than 150,000) at shutdown. The FBI arrested the administrator and ran the site itself for about two weeks, unmasking users with a hacking tool. The operation led to 956 arrests of users; Europol reported 368 suspects arrested or convicted in Europe alone by May 2017. The lead administrator was sentenced to 30 years in May 2017; two co-administrators got 20 years each.

n: Operation Atlantic — FBI and EU follow-up to Boylover network
who: Online offender networks incl. members of the Boylover network
d: A joint FBI–EU investigation coordinated by Europol from November 2010. By February 2012, 37 child sex offenders had been identified and 17 arrested for molestation and production of illegal content; 8 victims were identified. Two targets had been members of the Boylover network tackled in Operation Rescue.

n: Boystown darknet platform
who: Boystown (Tor platform, about 400,000 registered users)
d: Boystown launched in June 2019, focused on the abuse of boys, and had 400,000 registered users when a BKA-led taskforce with Europol, the Netherlands, Sweden, Australia, Canada and the US took it down in April 2021. Three German administrators were arrested in Germany and one German national in Paraguay. In December 2022 they were sentenced to between 7 and 12 years, two with preventive detention. Successor platforms with a common German administrator were shut down around Christmas 2022.

n: Nth Room and Doctor's Room — Telegram sexual blackmail rings
who: Telegram chatrooms 'Nth Room' (Moon Hyung-wook) and 'Doctor's Room' (Cho Ju-bin)
cover: A man's early 112 report was reportedly not treated as credible (Wikipedia, citation needed); two university students ('Team Flame') and journalists exposed it in 2019.
d: Operators blackmailed women and girls into producing sexual images and videos and sold access to Telegram chatrooms; at least 10,000 people used the 'Doctor's Room' chats, some paying up to $1,200. At least 74 victims, including 16 minors, were exploited there. After petitions signed by millions, police named the operator, Cho Ju-bin, in March 2020 — the first official identity disclosure for a sex offender in South Korea — and on 26 November 2020 the Seoul Central District Court sentenced him to 40 years (reported raised to 42 years on appeal in 2021). Moon Hyung-wook, who created the original 'Nth Room' chatrooms, was sentenced to 34 years by the Andong court on 8 April 2021. The law was changed to punish possessing and viewing such material.

n: AUSTRAC v Westpac — payments linked to child exploitation in the Philippines
who: Westpac Banking Corporation (failure to monitor transfers)
d: In November 2019 AUSTRAC alleged Westpac had breached anti-money-laundering law more than 23 million times, including failing to report international funds transfer instructions worth more than A$11 billion; the breaches included failures over suspicious transactions associated with possible child exploitation. The scandal forced the resignation of chief executive Brian Hartzer. On 24 September 2020 Westpac and AUSTRAC agreed a record A$1.3 billion penalty, the largest in Australian corporate history.

n: 764 network — founder sentenced to 80 years
who: 764 (online network on Discord/Telegram; founder Bradley Cadenhead)
d: 764, named after the first digits of the ZIP code of Stephenville, Texas, extorted minors into producing abuse material, self-harm and animal cruelty. Its founder, Bradley Cadenhead, was arrested in August 2021 aged 16 and on 16 May 2023 was sentenced in Texas to 80 years after pleading guilty to nine counts of possession/promotion of child sexual abuse material. The US DOJ describes 764 as a nihilistic violent extremist network and its Counterterrorism Section prosecutes it; on 29 April 2025 DOJ announced the arrests of two alleged leaders of the subgroup '764 Inferno', in North Carolina and in Greece. On 10 December 2025 Canada became the first country to list 764 as a terrorist entity.

n: France charges Telegram founder Pavel Durov
who: Telegram (messaging platform)
d: Durov was arrested at Le Bourget airport on 24 August 2024 and on 28 August a Paris investigating judge placed him under formal investigation on all the charges for which he was arrested, including suspected complicity in running a platform allowing illicit transactions, images of child sexual abuse, drug trafficking and fraud, and refusal to communicate information to authorities. He was released on 5 million euros bail, required to report to police twice a week and barred from leaving France. A BBC investigation that month found Telegram was not a member of NCMEC or the IWF and had ignored repeated requests to join. On 4 December 2024 the IWF announced Telegram would use its hashes of known abuse images to detect such material in public parts of the platform; the IWF said it had confirmed thousands of reports of abuse imagery on Telegram since 2022.

n: EU Child Sexual Abuse Regulation ('chat control') and interim derogation
who: European Commission, Council and Parliament
d: The Commission proposed the CSA Regulation (COM(2022) 209) to require platforms to assess risks and allow detection orders; it has been deadlocked over mandatory scanning. The interim derogation from the ePrivacy Directive (Regulation (EU) 2021/1232, in force 2 August 2021, extended in 2024) let providers voluntarily detect abuse material; with no agreement it lapsed on 3 April 2026. A new temporary derogation, Regulation (EU) 2026/1881, was adopted on 24 July 2026 and published 28 July 2026. As of October 2026 the permanent regulation has not been adopted.

n: Stanford finds abuse material links in LAION-5B AI training dataset
who: LAION-5B dataset (German non-profit LAION)
d: In December 2023 a Stanford Internet Observatory study found 3,226 suspected instances of child sexual abuse material in LAION-5B, a dataset used to train Stable Diffusion and other image generators, 1,008 of them externally validated. LAION, the German non-profit that created it, temporarily took down LAION-5B and LAION-400M to check them before republishing. NCMEC has reported that its 2025 CyberTipline data included more than 12,000 reports involving CSAM found in AI training data.

n: Regpay — Minsk-based paid abuse sites / Operation Falcon
who: Regpay Co. Ltd (Belarus) with Florida payment firm Connections
d: Regpay Co. Ltd of Minsk, Belarus, processed paid memberships to about 50 websites, including child abuse sites it operated itself, serving thousands of subscribers worldwide; payments were laundered with help from Connections USA of Fort Lauderdale, Florida. US Attorney General John Ashcroft announced the case in January 2004 as part of Operation Falcon. Regpay's president Yahor Zalatarou and marketing director Alexei Buchnev were arrested at a Paris hotel on 30 July 2003 after a ruse by US agents, and technical administrator Aliaksandr Boika was arrested in Tarragona, Spain, on 31 July 2003 and extradited. All pleaded guilty in New Jersey. Buchnev was sentenced to 40 months in May 2006; Zalatarou and Boika were each sentenced to 25 years on 9 August 2006. Connections' chief executive pleaded guilty to money laundering. Hundreds of subscribers were arrested in the US and other countries.

n: 'Kids the Light of our Lives' forum
who: Online chat forum with live streaming of abuse
d: An internet chat room, hosted from Buxhall in Suffolk, featuring images and live streams of the sexual abuse of children. Forensic teams found 75,960 indecent images on the host's computer and evidence he had supplied 11,491 images to other users. The trail began in Canada with the arrest of 24 offenders; in a 10-month operation by the Virtual Global Taskforce, led by the UK's CEOP and involving agencies from 35 countries, officers posed as the host and ran the chat room for 10 days. British authorities said on 18 June 2007 that more than 700 suspects had been identified worldwide and 31 children rescued, some only a few months old. The host, Timothy David Martyn Cox, admitted nine counts of possessing and distributing indecent images and was given an indeterminate sentence at Ipswich Crown Court that day.

n: DarkScandals site administrator arrested
who: DarkScandals (dark and clear web site)
d: A site on both the dark and clear web that advertised rape and blackmail videos of girls and included child abuse material (over 2,000 videos and images). After US IRS-CI, HSI and DOJ, Dutch police and FIOD, the BKA and Europol cooperated, Dutch police arrested the administrator at his home in Barendrecht on 9 March 2020 and the site was taken down.

n: Operation Tantalio — WhatsApp groups sharing abuse material
who: 25 invitation-only WhatsApp groups linked from Tor
d: Spanish National Police found Tor users being directed to invitation-only WhatsApp groups (25 under investigation). Action days on 28–29 March 2017 with Europol and Interpol led to 39 arrests in Europe and South America; more than 100 targets in 13 Central and South American countries were pursued through Interpol.

n: Operation Atlas — Virtual Global Taskforce P2P sweep
who: Peer-to-peer distributors and producers
d: Ten Virtual Global Taskforce members (Australia, Colombia, Netherlands, Switzerland, US HSI, Korea, New Zealand, Canada, UAE, UK) arrested 303 people suspected of distributing and producing abuse material and identified 106 victims, announced November 2015.

n: Gulf states block Roblox over child safety (2025)
who: Roblox Corporation
d: In August 2025 Qatar blocked access to Roblox (13 August) and Kuwait's telecoms regulator temporarily blocked it (21 August) after parents and community groups raised child-safety concerns; Turkey had blocked it on 7 August. Roblox had been banned in Oman and Jordan since 2020, and was banned in the UAE from 2018 to 2021. Wikipedia additionally reports that Bahraini MPs drafted a ban, Palestine announced a ban in November 2025, Kazakhstan's and Kyrgyzstan's authorities warned parents about predators, and Buenos Aires and three Argentine provinces blocked it on school devices after grooming reports.

n: Operation Soteria Shield (North Texas, 2025–2026)
who: FBI Dallas, North Texas ICAC Task Force, over 70 agencies, NCMEC
d: FBI Dallas and the North Texas Internet Crimes Against Children Task Force, with about 70 law enforcement agencies, ran the operation against online child exploitation. The first round, which began in April 2025 and lasted about a month, led to 244 people being charged and 109 children rescued, announced in June 2025. A second, two-month round, announced on 29 May 2026, led to 276 arrests and 89 children rescued across Texas, mostly on charges of possessing or distributing child sexual abuse material; authorities said cases remained active.

n: Kik Messenger — groups distributing abuse material
who: Kik Messenger
d: In March 2016 the arrest of a registered sex offender uncovered more than 200 Kik groups dedicated to distributing and selling child abuse material. A UK police investigator said delays in getting information from the company increased risk to children. Kik joined the Virtual Global Taskforce in 2015 and added image-detection in October 2016.

n: Rochdale — Operation Span convictions and 2024 review
who: Grooming network linked to two takeaway restaurants; Greater Manchester Police; Rochdale Council
cover: Police identified ring-leaders in 2007 but did not pursue them; Operation Span launched over two years after the first reports.
d: In May 2012 nine men were convicted after Operation Span, which Greater Manchester Police began in December 2010, more than two years after it was first told of abuse linked to two takeaways. Girls as young as 12 were plied with drink and drugs and passed between men for cash. A 173-page review published 15 January 2024 found children were 'left at the mercy' of gangs between 2004 and 2013 through a 'lamentable strategic failure' of senior police and council leaders; it identified hundreds of potential victims, mainly white girls from poor backgrounds, abused by Asian men, and said 96 men were still a potential risk to children.

n: Huddersfield — Operation Tendersea
who: Grooming networks; West Yorkshire Police investigation
d: In October 2018, 20 men were convicted at Leeds Crown Court of abusing girls as young as 11 in Huddersfield between 2004 and 2011; the ringleader's convictions involved 11 girls. By April 2023 Operation Tendersea had convicted 42 men in several trials for abuse between 1995 and 2013, with 505 years and six months of sentences.

n: Oldham — 2022 assurance review
who: Oldham Council; Greater Manchester Police; shisha bars, residential homes and taxis
d: The review published 20 June 2022 found 'serious failings' by Oldham Council and Greater Manchester Police: police and council knew of risks from shisha bars by late 2010 yet children of 13 and 14 still visited them in 2013, and multi-agency child-protection procedures were often not started. It criticised how a former council welfare rights officer, later convicted of rape and trafficking, was investigated. The review found no evidence of a cover-up by senior managers or councillors. Oldham is the first confirmed area for local investigation under the 2025 national inquiry.

n: Backpage.com — seizure, CEO plea and owners' convictions
who: Backpage.com classified advertising website
d: US authorities seized Backpage.com in April 2018. On 12 April 2018 CEO Carl Ferrer pleaded guilty to conspiracy to facilitate prostitution and money laundering; the Justice Department said the site earned hundreds of millions of dollars from 'escort' ads and that traffickers used it to advertise children and adults alike. In November 2023 a Phoenix jury convicted co-owners Scott Spear and John Brunst on Travel Act and money-laundering counts and Michael Lacey on one count of international concealment money laundering; co-founder James Larkin died on 31 July 2023 before trial. On 28 August 2024 Spear and Brunst were sentenced to 10 years and Lacey to five; DOJ said the scheme earned more than $500 million.

n: Carreto family — Tenancingo to New York trafficking
who: Carreto family pimping network based in Tenancingo, Tlaxcala
d: From 1991 to 2004 the Carreto family, based in San Miguel de Tenancingo, Tlaxcala, recruited young, poor women and girls in Mexico by deception and forced them into prostitution in brothels in Queens and Brooklyn, using rape, threats and forced abortion. Josue and Gerardo Flores Carreto were sentenced to 50 years each in April 2006 and Daniel Perez Alonso to 25 years. Their mother Consuelo Carreto Valencia was extradited in January 2007 and pleaded guilty to sex trafficking on 22 July 2008.

n: Canada — police-reported trafficking 2013–2023 (Ontario hub)
who: Mostly domestic traffickers known to victims
d: Statistics Canada reported on 1 November 2024 that police recorded 4,543 trafficking incidents from 2013 to 2023; about 23% of 3,558 victims were under 18 and 93% were women and girls. Ontario accounted for roughly two-thirds of incidents and Toronto alone for 20%. 91% of victims knew their trafficker and 34% were trafficked by an intimate partner; only 10% of completed adult court cases with a trafficking charge ended in a guilty decision.

n: IOM: up to 80% of Nigerian women and girls arriving in Italy may be sex-trafficking victims
who: Nigerian trafficking networks via Libya
d: In July 2017 the International Organization for Migration said perhaps 80 per cent of Nigerian migrant women and girls arriving by sea in Italy could be sex-trafficking victims, and that its Italy office had seen an almost 600 per cent rise in potential victims over three years. IOM indicators included age (most victims 13–24) and being 'controlled' by other migrants. Thomson Reuters Foundation later cited IOM data that Nigerian female arrivals rose from 1,500 in 2014 to more than 11,000 in 2016.

n: Operation Twisted Traveler — ICE crackdown on US offenders in Cambodia (2009)
who: US Immigration and Customs Enforcement; Cambodian police
d: In August 2009 three previously convicted US sex offenders arrested by Cambodian police in February — Ronald Boyajian, Erik Peeters and Jack Sporich — were returned to Los Angeles as the first defendants charged under 'Operation Twisted Traveler'. ICE head John Morton called Cambodia 'ground zero for child sex tourism'; ICE had stationed an agent in Cambodia full-time. Peeters was accused of abusing at least three Cambodian boys and Sporich of abusing a boy in Siem Reap (accusations at the time).

n: Senegal — forced begging and abuse of talibé children in Quranic schools (HRW 2019)
who: Some marabouts (Quranic teachers) running residential daaras
d: Human Rights Watch and the Senegalese PPDH platform reported on 11 June 2019 that over 100,000 talibé children in Senegal are forced by some Quranic teachers to beg daily, often under quotas enforced by beatings. For 2017–2018 they documented 16 deaths of talibés from beatings, neglect or endangerment, 61 cases of beatings, 15 cases of actual or attempted rape or sexual abuse and 14 cases of children chained or imprisoned, in 8 of Senegal's 14 regions. The 2025 US TIP report says the government identified 573 child forced-begging victims in the year.

n: The Gambia — child sex tourism on the Senegambia Strip (US TIP 2025)
who: Organized networks using European and Gambian travel agencies
d: The 2025 US TIP report says European tourists, primarily from the UK, reportedly travel to The Gambia to exploit children, and that organized sex-trafficking networks use European and Gambian travel agencies to promote the country as a destination, especially the Senegambia Strip. Women and girls from other West African countries, especially Nigeria, are recruited for tourism jobs and then sexually exploited. The Tourism Offences Act provides life imprisonment for child trafficking by tourists.

n: Tanzania — child sex trafficking in Zanzibar and cities (US TIP 2025)
who: Traffickers, brokers, foster families
cover: The report says the government did not adequately address corruption and official complicity.
d: The 2025 US TIP report says traffickers exploit children in sex trafficking, including by foreign offenders ('extraterritorial sexual exploitation'), and in forced labour and domestic servitude in Zanzibar, and that women and girls from the mainland are brought to Zanzibar with false promises. Child sex trafficking also occurs in Arusha, Dar es Salaam, Dodoma, Mbeya and Mwanza.

n: Zimbabwe — sex trafficking around gold and diamond mines; girls traded under ngozi (US TIP 2025)
who: Traffickers at mining sites; families
d: The 2025 US TIP report says traffickers exploit women and children in sex trafficking around mines, sometimes for money or food, and may exploit children as panners and ore couriers in gold and diamond mines. Traditional practices including trading daughters for food or money and ngozi — giving a relative to another family to atone for a killing — make girls vulnerable. Low-level official complicity persisted.

n: Ethiopia — girls trafficked to Djibouti, Sudan and Saudi Arabia (US TIP 2025)
who: Traffickers and begging rings
d: The 2025 US TIP report says traffickers exploit Ethiopian women and children in forced begging, sometimes via organized begging rings, in Saudi Arabia, and exploit Ethiopian girls in domestic servitude and sex trafficking in neighbouring countries, particularly Djibouti and Sudan, sometimes using drugs for control. Reports of official complicity continued.

n: Bangladesh — girls trafficked to India, Pakistan and the Gulf; Rohingya girls near Cox's Bazar (US TIP 2025)
who: Traffickers, recruitment agents, armed groups in Rohingya camps
cover: Corruption and official complicity were significant concerns; corrupt policing in Rohingya camps.
d: The 2025 US TIP report says traffickers exploit Bangladeshi women and girls in sex trafficking abroad, including in India, Pakistan and Gulf countries, and observers estimate children are 40 per cent of Bangladeshi sex-trafficking victims exploited abroad. Tourists have increased demand for sexual exploitation, including of Rohingya girls, near Cox's Bazar, where more than one million Rohingya refugees live in 33 camps. Courts convicted 103 traffickers, down from 407.

n: Swiss bar owner jailed 16 years for abusing more than 80 boys in Pattaya and northern Thailand
who: Unnamed Swiss national (72, from Lucerne) who ran a bar in Pattaya
d: A Swiss man previously convicted of abusing children in Fribourg (1980) and Valais (1991) returned to Thailand in 1996 and, mainly in 2002–2013, abused more than 80 boys in Pattaya, where he ran a bar with a hotel room frequented by Europeans, and in Nong Hoi in the north; he also forced boys to perform acts with European clients. Charged in Fribourg with human trafficking, encouraging prostitution, sexual acts with children and abuse material, he was sentenced by a Swiss court on 1 March 2018 to 16 years.

n: Philippines — foreign offenders and child sex trafficking in tourist towns (US TIP 2025)
who: Foreign offenders; family members; brothel and bar operators
cover: Corruption and official complicity remained significant concerns.
d: The 2025 US TIP report says sex trafficking frequently occurs in tourist destinations such as Boracay, Angeles City, Olongapo, Puerto Galera and Surigao. Many foreign offenders are convicted or charged sex offenders at home, most commonly from Australia, Japan, New Zealand, the UK and the US, with more reports from Canada, Morocco, Iraq and Denmark. Courts convicted 143 traffickers, 120 for sex trafficking.

n: Mongolia — girls sex-trafficked in Ulaanbaatar hotels and karaoke bars (US TIP 2025)
who: Traffickers in hotels, massage parlours, karaoke clubs
cover: The report says exploitation is sometimes facilitated by lack of police enforcement; some families are complicit.
d: The 2025 US TIP report says women and girls are sex-trafficked in Mongolian hotels, massage parlours, illegal brothels, bars and karaoke clubs, mostly in Ulaanbaatar, provincial centres and border areas, sometimes facilitated by a lack of police enforcement; traffickers use online platforms to groom and blackmail children; and children taken abroad for competitions have instead been put to work, e.g. as horse jockeys.

n: Cartagena — 'La Madame' network exploiting girls for tourists (plea 2018)
who: Liliana del Carmen Campos Puello ('La Madame')
cover: At hearings she threatened to reveal the names of politicians and powerful men she said were clients (her claim, unverified).
d: Liliana del Carmen Campos Puello ran a sex network from a Bocagrande apartment in Cartagena, supplying young women and minors to parties on yachts, in hotels and at beaches and sending women to Panama, Mexico, Miami and the Bahamas; prosecutors seized 15 ledgers of clients and payments, and a WhatsApp group listed 200 women. In 2018 she accepted charges of human trafficking and conspiracy in a plea deal and was sentenced to eight years and one month; she was released on parole in 2023. US ICE supported the investigation.

n: Peru — foreign tourists exploit children in Cusco, Lima and the Amazon (US TIP 2025)
who: Criminal groups transporting tourists on the Amazon
cover: Authorities charged two police officers for crimes against trafficking victims; corruption remained a significant concern.
d: The 2025 US TIP report says tourists from the US and Europe exploit children in Cusco, Lima and the Peruvian Amazon, and in Loreto criminal groups take foreign tourists by boat to remote venues on the Amazon River where women and children are exploited. Peruvian, Venezuelan and Bolivian women and girls are lured to mining and logging camps. Courts convicted 59 traffickers in 2024.

n: Paraguay — 47,000 children in criadazgo domestic servitude (US TIP 2025)
who: Families taking in children as unpaid domestic workers
d: The 2025 US TIP report says criadazgo — compelling children to work as domestic workers — is a common form of trafficking in Paraguay; an estimated 47,000 children are in criadazgo, mostly girls (boys are 30 per cent), and many are highly vulnerable to sex and labour trafficking. Colombia's report describes the same practice.

n: Honduras, El Salvador, Guatemala — gangs exploit girls; North American offenders (US TIP 2025)
who: Gangs and criminal organizations; foreign offenders
d: The 2025 US TIP reports say criminal organizations including gangs exploit girls in sex trafficking in urban Honduras and Guatemala, and that men from Canada and the US exploit Honduran children. In El Salvador, foreign tourists sexually exploit children and the rapid growth of tourism has created new risks; an estimated 140,000–200,000 Salvadoran children have a parent abroad or detained. Guatemalan children are exploited in Mexico and the US and in live-streamed abuse.

n: Romania — girls in state institutions at risk; victims sent across Europe (US TIP 2025)
who: Traffickers; staff of some government-run institutions
cover: Alleged complicity, misconduct and negligence by government employees in cases involving children in government-run homes remained a concern.
d: The 2025 US TIP report says most identified victims are women and girls exploited in Romania and in Austria, France, Germany, Italy, Spain and the UK; children in government-run institutions, particularly girls in homes for persons with disabilities, are at risk of sex trafficking; and Roma children as young as 11 are 'sold' into marriage. Courts convicted 161 traffickers (143 for sex trafficking) and 600 victims were identified in 2024.

n: Albania — children exploited in tourist season; first trafficking convictions since 2021 (US TIP 2025)
who: Traffickers; families
d: The 2025 US TIP report says traffickers exploit Albanian women and children in sex trafficking and forced labour, especially in tourist season; Roma and Balkan-Egyptian children are forced to beg; and Albanian migrants in Western Europe, particularly the UK, are vulnerable to forced criminality. Courts convicted two sex traffickers and two labour traffickers, the first convictions since 2021. In the UK, Albanians were the second most common nationality referred as potential victims in 2024 (2,492), 95 per cent as adults.

n: Lebanon — Chez Maurice and Silver-B: about 75 Syrian women freed from sex-trafficking ring (2016)
who: Chez Maurice and Silver-B brothels
cover: Chez Maurice was raided in late 2011 when a 17-year-old Syrian girl was found trapped there, closed for about three months and reopened. A survivor told Legal Agenda a trafficker claimed he had 'bought the state'.
d: In March 2016 Lebanese security forces freed as many as 75 Syrian women from two brothels, Chez Maurice and Silver-B, in the Maameltein red-light district of Jounieh, and arrested and indicted over a dozen people on sex-trafficking charges. HRW said Syrian refugee women were at particular risk and that the same premises had been raided in 2011, when a 17-year-old Syrian girl was found, and later reopened. Lebanon's police identified 87 trafficking victims in 2016, mainly these survivors.

n: UK — IICSA finds gaps let known offenders abuse children abroad (2020)
who: UK Home Office, police, courts
cover: IICSA found travel restrictions were rarely used: 11 of 5,551 Sexual Harm Prevention Orders in 2017/18 and six Sexual Risk Orders in force in March 2019.
d: The Independent Inquiry into Child Sexual Abuse report on the protection of children outside the UK (January 2020) found that only 11 of the 5,551 Sexual Harm Prevention Orders made in 2017/18 included foreign-travel restrictions, that 361 UK nationals sought consular help after arrest abroad for child sex offences in 2013–2017, and that there appear to have been only about eight successful UK prosecutions since 1997 for offences committed abroad, including Keith Morris (18.5 years, Kenya) and Mark Frost (Thailand).

n: Fr Johannes Rivoire — Oblate in Nunavut, never extradited from France
place: Arviat, Rankin Inlet, Naujaat and Whale Cove, Nunavut
who: Oblates of Mary Immaculate (OMI Lacombe Canada; Oblates of France)
cover: He left for France in January 1993; a Canadian arrest warrant followed in 1998 and charges were later stayed. A 2022 warrant led to an extradition request that French authorities denied. The 2024 Denis review found the RCMP never contacted the Oblates when charges were laid. In February 2024 the Vatican ruled against his dismissal. He died in France in 2024 without trial.
d: French Oblate Johannes Rivoire worked in the Canadian North from 1959 to 1993. He faced at least three sexual-abuse charges (1998 warrant) concerning Inuit children in Arviat, Rankin Inlet and Naujaat, and a 2022 warrant for indecent assault on a girl in Arviat and Whale Cove between 1974 and 1979. A March 2024 review by retired Quebec justice André Denis, commissioned by the Oblates, concluded on the preponderance of evidence that he assaulted six children. Inuit Tapiriit Kanatami called his death without trial in April 2024 'a systemic failure of nation states and religious institutions'.

n: Costa Rica — Fr Mauricio Víquez, convicted after fleeing to Mexico
who: Archdiocese of San José; Episcopal Conference of Costa Rica
cover: A San José civil court ordered Archbishop José Rafael Quirós, the Episcopal Conference and the church's property entity to pay 65 million colones; the victims' lawyer said the church knew from 2002 and did nothing. Three other complaints were declared time-barred.
d: Víquez, a former church spokesman on family issues, fled Costa Rica in 2018 when accusations surfaced, going via Panama to San Nicolás de los Garza, Mexico, where he was caught; he was extradited in 2021. The church expelled him from the clergy in 2019. In March 2022 he was sentenced to 20 years (6 for sexual abuse, 14 for rape) for abusing an 11-year-old boy in his parish in 2002–2003. In August 2022 a civil court ordered the archbishop and two church entities to pay about US$100,000 in damages.

n: Methodist Church (Britain) — Past Cases Review
who: Methodist Church in Britain
cover: The church said abuse by some Methodists had been ignored or not listened to; it issued an 'unreserved apology'.
d: Published on 28 May 2015 after three years of research, the Methodist Church's Past Cases Review found 1,885 cases of sexual, physical, emotional and domestic abuse or neglect going back to 1950. In 26% of cases church ministers or lay employees were identified as the alleged perpetrators. Six police investigations were ongoing. General Secretary Martyn Atkins made an unreserved apology.

n: Nigeria — Kaduna 'Islamic school' raid frees 300+ boys and men
who: Imam Ahmad Bun Hambal Centre for Islamic Studies (purported Islamic school / rehabilitation centre)
d: On 26 September 2019 Kaduna police raided a building signed as an Islamic studies centre and freed more than 300 boys and men, many chained and with whip scars. Some had been brought from Burkina Faso, Mali and Ghana; families said they were denied access. Seven people claiming to be teachers were arrested. Local media reported captives were tortured, starved and sexually abused. The raid led to further rescues from similar 'torture houses' in northern Nigeria.

n: Amish bishop charged for not reporting abuse confession (Lancaster County)
who: Old Order Amish church district, Lancaster County
cover: Witnesses said the bishop had the matter 'handled internally' to keep it quiet; the church excommunicated the abuser but did not notify police.
d: In April 2020 Amish bishop Levi Esh Sr., 63, was arraigned on felony and misdemeanour charges for failing to report a church member's confession to sexually assaulting three girls around 2012–2013. Pennsylvania law requires clergy to report child abuse.

n: Afghanistan — students report sexual abuse in Taliban-run madrasahs
place: Western and southwestern Afghanistan (incl. Farah Province)
who: Taliban-run madrasah system (6,836 male madrasahs per a Feb 2024 UN report)
cover: A 16-year-old said he reported a teacher to the school's qari, who only told the teacher to stop; the teacher admitted it and continued. The schools are run by the de facto Taliban authorities.
d: In March 2024 RFE/RL's Radio Azadi published accounts from male students aged 10 to 17 at Taliban-run madrasahs in western and southwestern Afghanistan who said teachers pressured them and classmates into sexual acts and used corporal punishment; some left school. The report cited a February 2024 UN report counting 6,836 Taliban-established madrasahs for boys and a decree seeking 100,000 new madrasah teachers.

n: Ryan Commission — industrial schools run by religious orders
who: Christian Brothers (most boys' institutions), Sisters of Mercy (most girls' institutions) and other Catholic orders
cover: Christian Brothers sued the commission in 2004 to keep members' names out; no real names of perpetrators published; findings not to be used for prosecutions; state Department of Education inspections failed
d: The Commission to Inquire into Child Abuse reported on 20 May 2009 after a nine-year investigation of more than 250 church-run institutions that held over 30,000 children from the 1930s to the 1990s. It found sexual abuse 'endemic' in boys' institutions run mainly by the Christian Brothers; the Sisters of Mercy ran most girls' institutions. The 2,600-page report names no perpetrators after a Christian Brothers lawsuit. A parallel state redress scheme paid about 12,000 people an average of €65,000.

n: Illinois Attorney General — clergy abuse report
who: Six Catholic dioceses of Illinois
cover: Before the investigation the dioceses had publicly listed only 103 substantiated abusers
d: Attorney General Kwame Raoul's report of 23 May 2023, from an investigation opened in 2018, named 451 Catholic clerics and religious brothers who abused at least 1,997 children in Illinois' six dioceses over decades. Before the inquiry the dioceses had publicly listed 103 substantiated abusers.

n: Michigan Attorney General — clergy abuse investigation
who: Catholic dioceses of Michigan
d: Attorney General Dana Nessel said on 23 December 2019 that the state investigation had identified 270 priests alleged to have abused 552 victims. Seven priests had been charged in 2019, two of whom had pleaded guilty. Most cases could not be prosecuted because of statutes of limitations.

n: Diocese of Ballarat — Gerald Ridsdale and Royal Commission Case Study 28
who: Catholic Diocese of Ballarat; Bishop Ronald Mulkearns
cover: Ridsdale moved through about 13 postings 1962–1991; Mulkearns knew by late 1975; a senior police officer in 1972 offered a detective promotion to stop investigating Monsignor John Day
d: Gerald Ridsdale, ordained 1961, was convicted in a series of trials from 1993 of abusing more than 70 children; he died in prison in 2025. He was moved between parishes including Mildura, Swan Hill, Warrnambool, Apollo Bay, Edenhope and Mortlake, then to Sydney. The Royal Commission's Ballarat report of 6 December 2017 found Bishop Mulkearns knew of his offending by late 1975 and still reappointed him, a 'catastrophic' failure. It also found police obstruction of a 1972 investigation of Monsignor John Day.

n: IICSA — Archdiocese of Birmingham
who: Roman Catholic Archdiocese of Birmingham
cover: Fr James Robinson moved parish after 1980s complaints, police not told; he fled to the US in 1985 and received archdiocesan payments for seven years; the Vicar General helped Fr Samuel Penney avoid arrest and leave the UK
d: The IICSA case study report of 20 June 2019 found more than 130 allegations against 78 people associated with the archdiocese since the 1930s. It examined priests James Robinson, Samuel Penney and John Tolkien. Robinson was moved to another parish after complaints in the 1980s without police being told, then fled to the US in 1985 while still receiving archdiocesan support; he was later extradited and jailed for 21 years.

n: Munich and Freising abuse report (Westpfahl Spilker Wastl)
who: Archdiocese of Munich and Freising; former archbishops incl. Joseph Ratzinger, Friedrich Wetter, Reinhard Marx
cover: Report found misconduct by archdiocesan leaders, including Joseph Ratzinger in four cases; only 4 of 173 accused priests were dismissed from the clerical state
d: The report commissioned by the archdiocese from law firm Westpfahl Spilker Wastl, published 20 January 2022, covered 1945–2019 and found at least 497 victims and 261 possible perpetrators and accomplices, 173 of them priests. It found misconduct by Joseph Ratzinger (Archbishop 1977–1982, later Pope Benedict XVI) in four cases, Cardinal Friedrich Wetter in 21 and Cardinal Reinhard Marx in two (the full report lists three). Ratzinger corrected his statement that he had not attended a January 1980 meeting about priest Peter Hullermann, who was admitted to Munich in 1980 and later reoffended.

n: Cardinal Groër affair and Klasnic victims' commission, Austria
who: Archdiocese of Vienna; Austrian Bishops' Conference; Independent Victims' Protection Commission (Klasnic Commission)
d: Archbishop of Vienna Cardinal Hans Hermann Groër stepped down in September 1995 after a former pupil, followed by others, accused him of sexual abuse; in 1998 Austrian bishops said they considered the allegations well founded, and the Holy See opened an inquiry. In spring 2010 the bishops set up the Independent Victims' Protection Commission chaired by Waltraud Klasnic. By 31 August 2021, according to the church's victims' foundation, payments had been approved in 2,550 cases, about €33 million in total. At Kremsmünster Abbey, the former head of the boarding school was jailed for 12 years in 2013 for crimes against 24 former pupils, 15 of them victims of sexual abuse.

n: University of Zurich pilot study — Catholic Church in Switzerland
who: Swiss Bishops' Conference and religious orders (commissioned study)
d: Historians at the University of Zurich, led by Monika Dommann and Marietta Meier and commissioned by the Swiss Bishops' Conference and religious orders, published a pilot study in September 2023 on sexual abuse in the Swiss Catholic Church since the mid-20th century. They documented 1,002 cases involving 510 accused people and 921 victims; 74% of the documents concerned abuse of minors. More than half the cases occurred in pastoral work and about 30% in Catholic children's homes, schools and boarding schools. The researchers called the cases 'the tip of the iceberg' and found that church criminal law was hardly ever applied, with many cases kept secret, covered up or trivialised.

n: Próvolo Institute, Luján de Cuyo (Mendoza) — convictions 2019
who: Provolo Institute for the Deaf (Argentina branch); Fr Nicola Corradi, Fr Horacio Corbacho, gardener Armando Gómez; Sr Kumiko Kosaka charged
cover: Corradi had been accused in Verona in 2009 yet continued at the Argentine school; Japanese nun Kumiko Kosaka charged with abuse and covering up
d: Priests Nicola Corradi (Italian) and Horacio Corbacho and other staff of the Provolo school for deaf children in Luján de Cuyo, Mendoza were arrested in 2016, charged with abusing at least two dozen students. On 25 November 2019 a Mendoza court convicted Corradi, Corbacho and gardener Armando Gómez of abusing children at the school between 2004 and 2016; the victims in the trial were 10 former students. Corradi was sentenced to 42 years, Corbacho to 45 and Gómez to 18. Nun Kumiko Kosaka was charged in 2017 with helping the abuse and with physically abusing students.

n: Marcial Maciel and the Legion of Christ — 2019 internal report
who: Legion of Christ (Legionaries); founder Marcial Maciel
cover: Letters to the Vatican in 1976, 1978 and 1989 and formal charges in 1998 produced no action; Vatican in 2010 said the Legion had shielded Maciel; Maciel never laicised or tried
d: For decades until 2006 the Vatican dismissed accusations by seminarians that founder Marcial Maciel had abused them. In 2006 it ordered him to retire to a life of 'prayer and penitence', and on 1 May 2010, after an apostolic visitation, it said his acts were 'true crimes'. The Legion's own report, released on 21 December 2019, found that 175 minors were abused by 33 of its priests between 1941 and 2019; at least 60 of them by Maciel. It said 111 of the 175 were victims of Maciel or of his victims, and that 14 of the 33 abusive priests had themselves been abused within the order.

n: Sacramentorum sanctitatis tutela / De delictis gravioribus (2001)
who: Holy See — Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith (Cardinal Joseph Ratzinger, prefect)
cover: All abuse-of-minor cases reserved to the CDF under pontifical secret
d: Pope John Paul II's motu proprio Sacramentorum sanctitatis tutela (30 April 2001), with the CDF letter De delictis gravioribus of 18 May 2001 signed by its prefect Cardinal Joseph Ratzinger, reserved to the CDF the delict of a cleric's sexual offence with a minor under 18, required bishops to notify the CDF after a preliminary investigation, and stated that such cases were subject to the pontifical secret, which remained until December 2019. In May 2014 the Holy See told the UN Committee against Torture that from 2004 to 2013 the CDF had studied 3,420 credible cases of abuse of minors and that 884 priests had been dismissed from the clerical state.

n: Pontifical secret lifted for abuse cases (December 2019)
who: Pope Francis
d: On 17 December 2019 Pope Francis issued the instruction 'On the confidentiality of legal proceedings', removing the pontifical secret from cases of sexual abuse of minors and vulnerable persons, child abuse material and concealment of such crimes. Information must still be treated with 'security, integrity and confidentiality' but can be made available to state authorities, and church officials were told to comply with civil laws. In a separate change the same day, the age limit in the Vatican's definition of child abuse material was raised from 14 to 18.

n: Fr Brendan Smyth — Norbertine order
who: Norbertine order (Kilnacrott Abbey); Fr Brendan Smyth
cover: Norbertines moved him between parishes, dioceses and countries without reporting him; at a 1975 church inquiry two boys signed oaths of silence; mishandled extradition by the Irish Attorney General's office contributed to the fall of the government in 1994
d: Norbertine priest Brendan Smyth abused children for decades from the 1950s in Northern Ireland, the Republic and the United States; the BBC put the number at at least 143. In 1975 Seán Brady, later Cardinal, attended church meetings where two teenage victims were sworn to secrecy; their evidence was never given to police. The Irish government's delay in acting on the RUC's extradition request led to the collapse of the Reynolds coalition in 1994. He was jailed in Northern Ireland in 1994 for abusing dozens of children there, and in July 1997 was sentenced in Dublin to 12 years for abusing 20 children in the Republic. He died in the Curragh Prison in August 1997. The Historical Institutional Abuse Inquiry (2017) found the Norbertine order moved him to another diocese despite knowing his history.

n: Scottish Child Abuse Inquiry — Smyllum Park and Bellevue (Daughters of Charity)
who: Daughters of Charity of St Vincent de Paul
d: About 11,600 children passed through Smyllum Park orphanage, run by the Daughters of Charity from 1864 to 1981. The inquiry's October 2018 findings said children were sexually abused by priests, a trainee priest, sisters, staff and a volunteer, and beaten with implements. Seventeen people were later charged; in 2025 the order agreed to pay up to £10 million.

n: Indian Residential Schools run by Catholic entities — TRC and papal apology
place: Maskwacis, Alberta (site of the 2022 papal apology)
who: Catholic dioceses and orders (incl. Oblates of Mary Immaculate) that ran about 44 of 80 schools at the 1931 peak (TRC says about 70% overall)
cover: Federal government funded and mandated attendance; Catholic entities cited lack of funds to compensate
d: More than 150,000 First Nations, Métis and Inuit children were forced to attend Canada's government-funded residential schools between the 1870s and 1997; the Catholic Church ran over half of them. In 2015 the Truth and Reconciliation Commission's chair said the commissioners had concluded that 'cultural genocide' was the best description of the system. In July 2022 at Maskwacis, Alberta, Pope Francis asked forgiveness 'for the wrong done by so many Christians to the Indigenous peoples', and on his return flight described the system as genocide.

n: Diocese of Stockton — Fr Oliver O'Grady
who: Diocese of Stockton; Bishop Roger Mahony (later Cardinal Archbishop of Los Angeles)
cover: After police declined to charge him in 1984, Bishop Mahony moved him to another parish and later made him pastor; Mahony said he was unaware of molestation reports, although a letter about earlier abuse was in O'Grady's personnel file.
d: Irish-born priest Oliver O'Grady, ordained in 1971 for the Diocese of Stockton, abused children from about 1973 and was moved between parishes. Bishop Roger Mahony knew of concerns by 1980 and moved him in 1984. O'Grady was convicted in 1993 and sentenced to 14 years; a 1998 civil jury awarded $30 million (reduced to $7 million). Paroled and deported to Ireland in 2000, he was convicted there for child abuse images in 2012 and 2020.

n: Maitland-Newcastle diocese — Fletcher, Cunneen inquiry and Archbishop Wilson (acquitted)
who: Diocese of Maitland-Newcastle; Archbishop Philip Wilson
cover: Monsignor Cotter's letter about Fr Denis McAlinden said 'we do not think it can be real serious'
d: A NSW Special Commission of Inquiry led by Margaret Cunneen SC, triggered by Detective Chief Inspector Peter Fox's public allegations in November 2012, reported on 30 May 2014. It found no evidence that senior police obstructed investigations, but found senior diocesan officials knew of complaints against Fr Denis McAlinden from 1954 and took over 40 years to tell police. On 22 May 2018 Newcastle Local Court found Archbishop of Adelaide Philip Wilson guilty of concealing abuse by Fr James Fletcher that a victim had told him about in 1976; on 6 December 2018 Judge Roy Ellis upheld his appeal, finding reasonable doubt, and quashed the conviction.

n: Fiji — transferred clergy and Julian Fox
who: Salesians; Catholic Church in Fiji
cover: Fox was transferred to Fiji in 1999 after Australian police began investigating; the Fiji church knew of allegations nine years before he was charged
d: Salesian priest Julian Fox was moved to Fiji in 1999 after Australian police began investigating abuse allegations; he was jailed in Australia in 2015. The Catholic Church in Fiji knew of the allegations nine years before he was charged. In July 2020 1News reported that some of about 1,300 alleged child abuse cases involving clergy in Fiji concerned clergy from Australia and New Zealand.

n: Slovenia — Fr Franc Frantar
who: Archdiocese of Ljubljana; Fr Franc Frantar
cover: Avoided prosecution by going to Malawi as a missionary until an Interpol notice was issued
d: Slovenian priest Franc Frantar was detained in 2006 for abusing up to 16 minors and later sentenced (sources give three and a half and five years). He first avoided prosecution by going to Malawi as a missionary and returned to Slovenia after Interpol issued a notice.

n: Belgium — Halsberghe commission (2000) and convictions
who: Catholic Church in Belgium
cover: In about half the 32 upheld cases the accused refused to appear; 31 cases were time-barred and only one reached court; in June 2010 police seized 450 internal dossiers from the Mechelen archbishop's palace
d: A church commission chaired by Godelieve Halsberghe from 2000 received over 300 complaints and upheld 32 of 33 formal ones; 31 were time-barred. Convictions included Fr Bruno Vos (nine years in 2009 for raping four minors), Robert Borremans (five years, 2008) and two Brothers jailed for ten years each in 2005 for abusing disabled people. On 24 June 2010 police raided the archbishop's palace in Mechelen, seizing 450 dossiers, and searched Cardinal Danneels' residence.

n: IICSA — Anglican Church investigation report
place: England and Wales (Church of England, Church in Wales)
who: Church of England; Church in Wales
cover: Inquiry found the Church gave 'excessive attention' to alleged perpetrators over victims, ignored safeguarding advice, and used forgiveness to justify failing to respond to allegations.
d: The Independent Inquiry into Child Sexual Abuse published its Anglican Church investigation report on 6 October 2020. It counted 390 convicted offenders associated with the Church of England from the 1940s to 2018 and warned the true scale cannot be known. In 2018 alone, dioceses received 2,504 safeguarding concerns, 449 of them about recent child sexual abuse. It found deference to authority, clericalism and taboos about sexuality kept victims from disclosing, and that bishops kept safeguarding decision-making power.

n: Royal Commission data — Anglican Church of Australia
who: Anglican Church of Australia
d: Data released at the Royal Commission into Institutional Responses to Child Sexual Abuse in March 2017 showed 1,082 people lodged complaints of child sexual abuse about 1,115 incidents in the Anglican Church of Australia between 1980 and 2015. The complaints identified 569 alleged perpetrators who were clergy, teachers or volunteers, plus 133 whose church roles were unknown (702 in total).

n: Frank Houston — Royal Commission Case Study 18 (Assemblies of God / Hillsong)
who: Assemblies of God in Australia (now Australian Christian Churches); Hillsong Church
cover: When allegations surfaced in 1999, Brian Houston, then National President of the Assemblies of God and Frank Houston's son, confronted his father, who confessed; Brian Houston and the National Executive did not refer the matter to police.
d: Pastor Frank Houston sexually abused a young boy in the 1970s. The Royal Commission's Case Study 18 findings (November 2015) found that Brian Houston and the national executive did not report the allegations to police when they emerged in 1999, and that Brian Houston had a conflict of interest as both national president and the son of the alleged perpetrator. Frank Houston died in 2004 without being charged.

n: Warren Jeffs — FLDS child 'marriages' conviction
place: Yearning For Zion ranch, Eldorado, Texas; Short Creek (Colorado City AZ / Hildale UT)
who: Fundamentalist Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-Day Saints (FLDS)
d: FLDS president Warren Jeffs was added to the FBI Ten Most Wanted list on 6 May 2006 and arrested in Nevada on 28 August 2006. A 2007 Utah conviction for accomplice to rape was reversed in 2010, and Arizona charges were dismissed in 2010. In August 2011 a Texas jury convicted him of two counts of sexual assault of a child, girls aged 12 and 15 he had taken as 'spiritual wives', and he was sentenced to life plus 20 years. Texas authorities had raided the YFZ ranch on 7 April 2008 and taken custody of about 416 children, who were later returned after courts found the removal unjustified.

n: Yaakov Litzman — breach of trust for shielding Malka Leifer
who: Israeli Ministry of Health; ultra-Orthodox Agudat Yisrael party
cover: A government minister pressured ministry psychiatrists to alter evaluations of an extradition suspect.
d: Former Israeli health minister Yaakov Litzman signed a plea deal in January 2022 admitting breach of trust for pressuring Health Ministry employees to change psychiatric evaluations so that Malka Leifer would appear unfit to stand extradition trial. He resigned from the Knesset in June 2022 and on 8 August 2022 the Jerusalem Magistrate's Court sentenced him to eight months' probation and a fine of about US$900. Australian Jewish groups condemned the deal as lenient.

n: Pennsylvania grand jury — Jehovah's Witnesses child sexual abuse charges
place: Harrisburg, Pennsylvania (defendants from Philadelphia, Delaware, Butler and Berks counties)
who: Jehovah's Witnesses congregations in Pennsylvania
d: A statewide investigating grand jury in Harrisburg, opened after a county prosecutor's referral, heard dozens of witnesses about abuse in Jehovah's Witness congregations. On 7 July 2023 Attorney General Michelle Henry announced charges against five more men, bringing the total to 14 charged; one earlier suspect killed himself before arrest. One former elder was later convicted in Lancaster County.

n: Argentina raids on The Family (Children of God) communes
who: The Family / Children of God
d: On 1 September 1993 Judge Roberto Marquevich ordered raids on Family communes near Buenos Aires; 137 children were taken into state custody and about 30 members arrested. The judge said nine children showed signs of 'cruel and atrocious maltreatment', which the group disputed. Children were later released after examination and no convictions resulted. Raids in Australia (1992, including Panton Hill, Victoria), France and Spain also ended without convictions.

n: Royal Commission Case Study 22 — Yeshivah Melbourne and Yeshiva Bondi
place: Yeshivah Centre, East St Kilda (Melbourne) and Yeshiva Centre, Bondi (Sydney)
who: Yeshivah Centre / Chabad Institutions of Victoria; Yeshiva Centre – Chabad NSW
cover: The Commission found that the principle of mesirah (not informing on a fellow Jew to secular authorities) as applied in the community discouraged reporting, and survivors who went to police were treated as outcasts. Bondi's Rabbi Yossi Feldman testified he 'was not aware it was illegal to touch a child's genitals'; the Commission found him ignorant of the duty to report.
d: The Royal Commission held hearings in February 2015 on responses to abuse by David Cyprys, David Kramer and Aron Kestecher at Yeshivah Melbourne and Daniel Hayman at Yeshiva Bondi. Its report (released October–November 2016) found 'a marked absence of supportive leadership' for survivors at Yeshivah Melbourne. Its 2017 final report recommended Jewish institutions state that mesirah does not apply to reporting child sexual abuse.

n: Royal Commission data — Uniting Church in Australia
who: Uniting Church in Australia
d: At a Royal Commission hearing on 10 March 2017, the Uniting Church was reported to have faced about 2,500 allegations of child sexual abuse over its 40-year history (it was formed in 1977). The Commission's Case Study 23 also examined Knox Grammar School, a Uniting Church school in Sydney.

n: Terry Knight — Diocese of Portsmouth
who: Church of England, Diocese of Portsmouth
cover: Bishop Timothy Bavin did not report Knight to police when parents raised concerns in 1985.
d: Terry Knight, active in the Diocese of Portsmouth, was convicted of child sexual offences in 1996 and again in 2016. Parents had raised concerns with the bishop in 1985, who did not inform police.

n: Independent Fundamental Baptist churches — Star-Telegram investigation
place: IFB churches in the US and Canada
who: Independent Fundamental Baptist churches and institutions
d: A Fort Worth Star-Telegram investigation published in December 2018 identified 412 allegations of sexual misconduct in 187 Independent Fundamental Baptist churches and institutions across 40 US states and Canada, some dating back to the 1970s. Reporters spoke to more than 200 current or former members, and described accused men being able to move to other churches through informal networks of church-college alumni.

n: Global Ikhwan (GISB) children's homes — Operation Global
place: Selangor and Negeri Sembilan (later raids in 8 more states)
who: Global Ikhwan Services and Business Holdings (GISB), linked to the banned Al-Arqam movement
d: On 11 September 2024 Malaysian police raided 20 charity homes linked to GISB Holdings in Selangor and Negeri Sembilan, rescued 402 children aged 1 to 17 and arrested 171 adults, after six months of intelligence work; police said they had received 41 reports about the group since 2011. By 10 October police put the total rescued at 625. Three madrasah student assistants in Kuala Pilah were charged with 14 counts of sexually abusing five children in 2022–2023, another teaching assistant with sexually assaulting four boys, and others with physical abuse of children; police said the investigation pointed to organised crime and human trafficking.

n: Mamou Alliance Academy — missionary children's boarding school, Guinea
who: Christian and Missionary Alliance (C&MA)
cover: Alumni wrote to C&MA headquarters about abuse from the 1980s for about ten years before an inquiry was set up.
d: Mamou Alliance Academy boarded the children of C&MA missionaries in West Africa. After 30 alumni asked for an investigation in 1995, an independent commission of inquiry heard 80 testimonies and reported in April 1998 that the denomination had been negligent; it identified nine offenders, and abuse included sexual molestation and rape. The US C&MA board issued an open letter asking victims' forgiveness.
